WHITTIER AN THE AMERICAN WAR.—Whittier, a Quaker, and, of course, an advocate of peace, was in great distress while the war continued. He had hoped that an appeal to arms !night have been averted. He would have been willing, as probably many in the North would have been willing, that the Government should pay. an indemnity to the slave-owners. But his was not the cowardly view of war; by nature he was bold and resolute. Lowell painted him long ago in some vigorous lines: " There is Whittier. whose swelling and vehement heart Strains the strait-breasted drab of the Quaker apart. And reveals the live man, still supreme and erect, 17nderneath the bemusamying wrappers of sect. After a weary time the end of the war came, and slavery was for ever destroyed La momentous fact of ,which the world has not felt, and will not for centuries feel, the full significance. The triumph of Whittier was not in the victory of ,Northern over Southern-born men, not in the downfall of -the Confederacy, but in the establish- ment of right and justice. When the proclamation of free i freedom carne he gave utterance to his long pent-up f,,elings n a poem of almost painful energy, fitly eg- t tied " LausDeo!" It is a cry of devout gratitude for i deliverance, n simple unaffected lines, which could scarcely have come from any other living man. Later, when the consequences of the great events began to loom up with the grandeur of mountains in the distance, he wrote "My Triumph." He hada right to exult. or ever thirty years he had devoted his life and strength to the cause, had voluntarily renonnePd fame, had chosen poverty, aed denied himself the pleasures which man holds dear in this life, and now his reward had come.— " Good Words" for January. • • 1 "Oh, it as a cra'el shame, Matt." r " Well, it, was a thigtake; for yesterday Sanr went to Kendall, and there, in AM, Stramon-gate,: he met Tom Philipson,who is just hoine from India: And what does 1 Tom say but, Have you seen the General yet ?' and, 'Great man is General Denton,' and Is it true that he is going to buy the Derwent estate?' and 'Won't the Indian I Government -miss General Denton!' Sam wasn't going to let Tom see how the land lay, and Tom went off'' saying that Sam had no call to be so peaky proud; that it wasn't him who had conquered the Maltrattas and taken the Ghiznee Pass." Jennie was crying bitterly, and saying softly to her- self "0 my brave laddie! 0 my bonnie lile Davie!" , "Hush, woman! •No good comes of crying. Write now as soon as you like, and the sooner the better." In a very few hours Jennie had acted on this advice,' and though the writing and spelling were wonderful, the poor sick General, nursing himself at the Bath waters, felt the love thatspoke in every word. He had I not expected much from his brothers; it was Jennie and Jennie's bairns be wanted to see. He was soon afterl Wards en honoured guest hi Esthvraite Grange; and the I handsome old soldier' riding slowly Snaring the lovely dales, surrounded by his nephews and nieces, became a well-kaown sight to the villages around, Many in Thirlston rememberel and none of his old companions found th.`...'enSelves forgotten. Nor did he' neglect his bretheril. These cautious men had be- come of late years manufacturers, and it was said were growing fabulously rich. They had learned the value the low coppice woods on their fell-side, and ba:a Started a bobbin-mill, which Sant superintended; while Matt Was on constant duty at^the tlteat steam-mill on Milloch- Force, where he spun his own' wools into blankets and eetges. - The rem were not insensible to the honour of their 'brother's career; they made great capital of it privately. But they were also istensely dissatisfied at the reckless way in which he spent his wealth. Young David Esth- Waite had joined a crack regiment with his uncle's intro- duction and at'his uncle's Charges, and Jennie and Mary Esthwaite had been what the brothers considered ex- travagantly•dowered in order that they might marry two poor clergymen whom they had set their hearts on. "it is just sinful, giving women that much good gold," said Matt, angrily; "and here we are needing it to keeps great business afloat." It was the first time Matt had dared to hint that the mill under his care was not making money, and he was terribly shocked when Sam made a similar confession. In fact, the brothers, with all their cleverness and industry, were so ignorant that they were necessarily at the mercy of those they employed, and they had fallen into roguish hands. Sam proposed that David should be asked to look over their affairs and tell them where the leakage was: "He was always a lile-hearted chap, and I'd trust him, Matt, up hill and down dale, I would." But Matt objected to this plan. He said David must be taken through the mills and the most made of every- thing, and then in a week or two afterwards be offered a partnership; and Matt, being the eldest, carried the day. A great festival was arraeged, everything was seen to the best advantage, and David was exceedingly interested. He lingered with a strange fascination among the steam-looms, and Matt saw the bait had taken, for as they walked back together to the old homestead, David said," You were ever a careful man, Matt, but it must take a deal of money—you understand, brother—if you need at any time—l hope I don't presume." "Certainly not. Yes we are doing a big business—a very good business indeed; perhaps when you are stronger you may like to join us.' "1 shant get stronger, Matt—so I spoke now." Sam, in his anxiety, thought Matt had been too pru- dent ; he would have accepted Davie's offer at once; but Matt was sure that by his plan they would finally get all the General's money into their hands. However, the very clever always find some quality that they have failed to take into account. After this long day at the mills General Denton had a severe relapse, and it was soon evident that his work was nearly finished. / "But you must not fret, Jennie dear,", he said cheer- fully; " f am indeed younger in years than you, but then I have lived a hundred times as long. What a stirring, eventful life I have had! I must have lived a cycle among these hills to have evened it; and most of -my comrades are already gone." One day, at the very last, he said," Jennie, there is one bequest in my will may astonish you, but it is all right. I went to see her a month ago. she is a widow now, with a lot of little lads around her. And I loved her, Jennie—never loved any woman bet her. Poor Mary! She has had a hard time; I have tried to make things, easier." "You had always a lile heart, Davie; you could do no, wrong to anyone." "I hope not. I—hope—not." And with these words and a pleasant smile the Gemmed answered some call that he alone heard, and trusting in his Saviour, passed con-. fidently The quick/3 and drift that fill the rift 'Between this world and heaven. His will, written in the kindest spirit, caused a deal of angry feeling; for it was shown by it that after his.viSit to the Danton Mills he had revoked a bequest to the brothers of £20,000, because, as he explicitly said, "My dear brothers do not need it ; " and this £20,000 he left to Mary Butterworth Pierson, "who is poor and delicate, and does sorely need it?' And the rest of his property he divided between Jennie and Jennie's,baims. In the first excitement of their disappointment and ruin, Sam, who dreaded his brother's anger, and who yet longed for some sympathetic word, revealed to Jennie and her husband the plan Matt had laid, and how signally it had failed. I told him, squire, I did for -sure, to be plain and honest with Davie. Davie was always a lile fellow, and he would have helped us out of trouble. Oh, dear! oh, dear ! that £20,000 would just have put a' things right." .

'Looming bastions fringed with fire. out of which the lightnings flashed from time to time. After nightfall I went to see the wrecked boat, lying in its house near the shore. There was something very shadowy and ghostly in the sight of the doomed craft seen by the doubtful light of a wax candle. We climbed the sides and stood among the vacant seats, ropes, and tackle, and heard from the boat's landsman of the preparations for the fatal voyage. The tiller ropes hang slack where they had slipped from her cox- swain's grasp, the rocket boxes were empty, the com- pass was gone, and the mast had broken away and dis- appeared. It was a suggestive sight; there hung the life-ropes which were powerless to save, and there were the seats of those of whom as Charles' Kingsley would say, "Verily, they .have gone ,down into Hades, even many stalwart souls of heroes." In looking at the boat I realised in a greater degree the feeling once aroused by the sight of a derelict boat towed into Tenby harbour, a shipwrecked waif of the sea, forsaken and with a branch of a tree lying in it, which seemed to have been used as an oar. As I walked from the boat- house along the snow-whitened shore, I could hear The plunging seas draw backward from the land and from somewhere above the waves, the melancholy piping note of an unseen solitary sea-bird. There was a somewhat brighter outlook on the fol- lowing day as I stood by the pier and talked with a man who was scanning the sea with that inquiring wistful look which one notices in the faces of those who dwell on the coast, a look, which does not belong to the land, and which only the mysterious sea can call up. He I was looking toward the distant wreck as if be expected to see something drift from that direction. Doubtless he was thinking of the missing man who was still lying somewhere under the waves, "tossing with tangle and with shells."

As I talked with him, there perched close by us on the pier wall a beautifully feathered full-throated throstle, which seemed to eye us inquisitively. It was a more hopeful omen than if a stormy petrel had come that way, for the throstle is a bird of whose song the poet says, _

And in the midmost heart of grief The passion clasps a secret joy. It was songless, it is true, in this sharp season, but by and bye its "warble liquid sweet" would be ringing "Eden through the budded qnicks," and telling to sor- rowing souls ho*:!every winter turns to spring. If it had a voice now perhaps it would be to the sea winds it would sing, and the burden of its song, I take it, would be—

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

I 'The fortnightly meeting of the Prescori Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Vi'histon, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present—Mr. John Lowe (chairman), Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. James Buckley, Joseph Jackson,james Burchall,John Whalley, Joseph Elli- son, William Middlehurst, Williath Dame, Charles B. John- Tyier. E. Syder. J. Kenwright, T. F. Hill, P. Longthn, Peter Middlehnrst, J. W. Wareing, and S. H. .Hartley (clerk.) RELIEF RETURNS. -- The Workhouse Master reported there were 494 inmate; of the house this week, against.49o last week, and 484 ite the corresponding week of last year; vagrants relieved were •34, corresponding week last year 60. Tun CAStAL WARD FOR T. REIAINS QUESTION.—MI. .Longtori aeked if the relieving officers at St. Helens were empoweiel to give a poor person 43 or 61 for a night's. lodgings when that person arrived la Bt. Helens late at night 7—The Clerk said they could not, as it wopld be con- trary to the orders of the Local Government Board.—Mr; Middlehurst said he had made inquiries in St. Helens, and he found that the number of such cases for the past year 'was only 30. It would require a tremendous expenditure to keep ,up an establishment in St. Helens for such eases, and therefore hp thought it was not worth while saving any more about it. THE WATER SUPPLY.—The Clerk stated that the Rev. Thomas Chambare had given notice that that day he would move "That steps be taken for immediately providing an adequate supply of water to the workhouse to be available in the event of fire." A letter had been received from that rev. geatleman apologising for inability to attend, and ask- ing that the matter be adjourned for a fortnight.—This was agreed to. Permits Ltnearics.—Respectio4 the maintenance of paupers in lunatic asylums, communications were read as follows :—From Rainhill Asylum, the Clerk etating that he was hardly in a position to answer an inquiry respecting the charge for maintenance from the let inst. He, how- , ever, thought he might safely say that there would-be no increase, but whether the committee would sanction a re- daction he was unable to say, as they might think It un- desirable in View of the large expense.; which would be incurred in opening the new annexe, an event which would shortly take place. The other letter was from Whlttingham Asylum, stating that there would be no change fer some time in the charge, which would remain at Is 7d. THE WATCHMAKERS' GRIEVANCES.—The Clerk read . a letter from Mr. James Robinson, secretary to the Preempt Watch Trade Association, enclosing the following copy of a resolution passed at a public meeting of the association on December 29:—" That, in the opinien of this meeting, the success of the watchmakers' deputation, which waited upon the Board of Trade on the 15th December, is mainly owing to the action taken by the Preecot Board of Guardians end their clerk, Mr. R. H. Hartley, and that the best thanks 'of the association be accorded to them for their efforts to assist the watchmakers." THE EMIGRATION OF CHILDREN.—MI. Tyrer asked whether anything had been heard from Canada as to the whereabouts of children who had been sent from that Union.—The Clerk replied nothing bad been heard up to the present. They had received no reply from the persons who were in charge, and other Boards of Guardians were in the same position. The department at Ottawa had not pro- perly organised their visiting arrangements.—Mr. Longton said he considered its very important coestion.—Mr.Tyrer remarked that he thought they.ought to know something of what became of the children.

nviL Tun I sami las Dozen PATIENT AGAIN.—Mr. Ware- ing said: want to ask the clerk what has been done with regard to th question of the removal of patients to the St. Helens Infections Hospital: Hata charge been agreed upon 7—The Clerk : It has not, Mr. Wareing,—Mr. Ware- lug: We have not heard anything about it foir some time. I don't know how the matter stands,—The Clerk: It comes to this ,• that the thardians are prepared to relieve all cases of destitution in St. Helens, but not to provide any ac- commodation which is likely Co prevent the spread of disease. That is a duty which does not devolve upon the Guardians. We have heard nothing from the St. Helens Corporation. This is very unsatisfactory, but the Guardiaas have done everything they possibly could—they have offered a reasonable enun.—Tbe matter then dropped. " DAINTY " l'utrStrna.—The Chairman: I am sure you will all agree with me that we all feel it a very great pleasure that Father Finegan has been promoted to the hon- ourable appointment of Dean. I am sure we all wish him success. (Applause.)—Mr. Dame: There cannot be a Sec- ond opinion as to that. Now you will have a Dean and a Daine on this Board. , (Laughter.)—Tho Clerk : Who 'deigns" to say that. (Renewed laughter.)---The Rey. Father Finegan: I am very much obliged to you. The meeting then closed. PEnsows

The next letter from Mr. Pardey he Mr. Worslev is dated ' Bth November, and reada as follows :—'• Wargrave-road.— I have read With considerable surprise the newspaper reports of the proceedings of the Newton Improvement Commis. Conons at. their meeting on Monday last. You called upon me to discuss a deviation from the first proposal. , At our previous meeting I complained that no plam had been sub- mitted to me, and that it was unreasonable to expect me to go into the subject without first being supplied with plan, and you promised that I should have plan. That promise was never fulfilled, but I am again called on (about half an hour before the Board meetine),with an aereement or heads of an agreement, and am asked to go into the question, and consent to the terms proposed, although no plan had pre- viously • been submitted. I, therefore,- in the pres3nce of Mr. Clark most distinctly and emphatically declined to die. cuss the question officially. You then remarked that we might talk over the matter, as you had a little time to spare, before the Board met. I consented, saying that any- thing which passed must be without prejudice. The re; port which I expected would have been given to your Board, the only one which should have been given, was that I declined to go into the wstion without first having plan. Why was this withheld from the Board, or if made to them in committee, why suppressed at the Board meet.' beg, when the reporters were present, unless with a view to create a prejudice in the minds of the leubliet ?" ,To this letter Mr. Worsley replied on the 10th- November. "What you told me when I saw you on the 4th ult. was that you had decided that ,inasmuch as you denied the necessity of the widening and the making of Wargrave-road south of the church gate. Mr. Legh would not give any land for the purpose of widening the road, nor would Mr. Loeb pay any part of the cost of mating the road- from that point, bat that up to the church gate, where. the road had been taken dyer by the district, Mr. Legh would give the land required. with such deviation as might be found necessary to adoid 'interference with existing buildings, This you stated to be your final decision, and this I, as in duty bound, reported to the special meeting of the Commissioners held the same day for the purpose of receiving a report of my negotiations with you as to the making of the road south of the church gates under an agreement. It is not a fact that the report which should have been „riven to the Board was that you declined to go into the question without a plan. It is not a fact that, I withheld that or any other report Made by you to me front the Board. I am much surprised that you should have written the ?otter I ant now with much regret acknowledging. P.S.—As corroborative evidence of the facts. I beg to refer you to my letter te you of the Ist of October, and to Your reply to me of the 2nd." Mr. PARDEY replied at some length on the 15th Novem: bar, sod reiterated his statement as to what took Place at the interview between Mr. Worsley and himself. He adds that "During this interview I asked if ' Canon Whitley had consented to give what land was required of him and agreed to the terms, and your reply was • I believe he does not object.' I have since ascertained that he had never been spoken to on the subject. I was desirous that Mr. Clark should be present at our interview, and called him into my office. You persistently requested an acceptance of the proposals, and I firmly adhered to my resolve not to discuss them, by reason of the plan being withheld. You put nD your papers and rose to go away, and Mr. Clark then left the room. You, however, before leaving, re- marked that you bad a few minutes to spare, and Suggested that it might facilitate matters for our next interview if we had a little talk over the questions. I consented, but with this remark, 'Our conversatioa must be understood to be without prejudice.' We then had a long desultory conver- sation, in which I gave my individual opinion, that looking at the facts as explained by you (that the Commissioners, did not contemplate making any road improveintliment be- yond the first two houses in the "Vulean"—ene of which is occupied by the manager, who is also Chairman of your Board of Commissioners), the proposed outlay was uncalled for. The ostensible reason was to provide a better road opersons going to And from the Vul.• can,f rthe and rgndlalae numberdmit that to f they are entitled to consideration. The densely populated portion of the Vulcan district is, I , believe, at a deit ince of from 500 to 750 yards from the two dwelling•houses above referred to,end they have to continue to wade through mud and dirt until they arrive at the manager's house. I told you, that, as a ratepayer, I felt it a pity there was not a ratepayers' protection association to , raise its voice against useless expenditure. I .did also , farther, add that if the deviation, as exp!ained by you, was I insisted on. I felt that it would be very prejodicial to Mr. Logic's property, and in that case I should advise Mr. Legh not to give land south of the Church gates. In conclusion, 1 I must add that I still expected a plan would be furnished, and that there would be a discussion thereon, yours obe- diently," The two last letters are one from Mr. VVoreley, dated 7th December, in which that gentleman says that "At a meet- ing of Commissioners held yesterday, after the general busi.' noes was transacted, I brought before the Board your letters to me alleging that I withheld from the Board a proper re- port respecting our interview as to Wargraveirnad. After a long discussion the following resolution was unanimously passed :—'Resolved, that the Commissioners support the law clerk in the report given by him to this Board of the interview with Mr. Pardey respecting Wargrave-road, and that the law clerk be requested to write to Mr. Pardey in- forming him of this resolution; and further, stating that Mr. Pardey has, its the opinion of the Commissioners, obstructed every work taken in hand by them for the good of the dis- trict, by which they were brought into contact with him; and further, that the law clerk be instructed to suggest to Mr. Pardey that this should be dis- continued; and further, that the Commissioners are still prepared, as they always have been, to enter into an agreement with Mr. Legh for the very necessary repairs to Wargrave-rood." The other and final letter is from Mr. Pardee to Mr. Worsley, dated 9th December, and states as follows :—I have this morning received your letter of the 7th test, inclosing copy of resolution passed by the Newton Improvement Commissioners on the previous day. Such resolution being founded on an ex-parte and incorrect report is one that I can well ignore with one remark, 'That when the Commissioners, through their officials, are prepared to do business in a business-like manner, they will be met in the same way, but lam not prepared at their dictation to depart from that rule.' I may add that at our last inter- view I, from previous experience, and advisedly, bad a witness present, and that I am prepared to substantiate the statements made by me in my letter of the 15th No- vember.

GENERAL NEWS.

On Wednesday the German Military Bin again CAMS be- fere the committee of the Reichstag, but no understanding was arrived at between the Government and the majority. ritA telegram from Vienna, dated Wednesday says :—There has been a wholesale expulsion of Austrian Jews from the ttussian frontier town of Woloozyka and from Odessa. In the London Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, a receiv- ing order was made against the estate of Count Henry Von Ebersberg, described as a manufacturing chemist, of 90, Cannon-street. The "Dublin Expiess's" London correspondent says: —"Mr. Parnell intends moving an amendment censuring the conduct of the Executive, evidence beimg accumulated for this purpose." The emigration returns for the past year, prepared by Mr. Giffen, show that daring the twelve months 233,119 persons left the United Kingdom, against 207,644 in the preceding year. DEATH FROM PRIVATION.—The Glasgow police reported on Thursday morning that Martin Cummings, a labourer, aged 45, was found dead near some waggons in Watson. street on Wednesday, having perished from privation and etposure. At Altrincham, on Thursday, F. Aylesbury and J. Robin- son, gamekeepers in the employment of Lord Egerton, were committed for trial at Chester_on the charge of feloniously wounding several men who had been detected in tae act of poaching. , • Sacreir.rox IN GVERNSEY.—The Castel Parochial Church land the Wesleyan Chapel, St. Peter's Port, both in tiller- ! neey, have been broken into and damaged. At the former place the thieves stole the contents of the poor box and a lquantity of sacramental wine. SHOCKING DISCOVERV.—On Sunday afternoon two men -were found dead, and in a charred condition, on a smoulder- ing cinder mound at Walsall. One was identified as Thomas I Rawson, the other is unknown. The place had been re- sorted to by homeless vagrants. ' OHRAFENT HoUNE In the city for Glue, China, Otleuts.l Wares, and Fancy Gonda.-171. Oxford-street, Manchester.— Adrt. CHILDERS AND HIS CONSTITUENTS.—A felegram was received in Edinburgh on Thursday morning from Mr. Childers stating that owing to his having caught a severe cold he would be unable to go to that city on Thursday. PROFESSIONAL MCSICIANS.—The firat annual provincial conffirence of members of the National Society of Profet- sional Musicians was opened on Wednesday at Birmingham, to which town the delegates were welcomed by the Mayor. I am sure you will allow a little of your space for the ventilation of a question closely connected with the happiness of those around us. It seems to the present writer that, although we have the poor always with us, the poverty, and unhappiness of the poor always give out a keener emphasis during the frosts and snows of winter. It is then that the depths of poverty make themselves more apparent: I wonder how many amongst us try to find out the. deeper depths. Year after year we go on accepting makeshift expedients for alleviating the misery of the unfortunate, the wealth of .the country grows in magnitude; it is said that bank deposits and building clubs were never in a more prosperous state. Listen to Mr. Giffin, and the political econo- mists, and one would think the heading to this let- ter entirely out of prace. Yet it is not so; the ex- perience of workingmen, if placed -before your I readers, would prove that not only does poverty 14exist, but that there is poverty that rarely receives ice, and that is rarely known by those who dis- pense the charity of the benevolent. vralA your readers to follow me with a sym- pathy that may leave criticism behind, while I point out i:ovr working-men, by subscription, and by forethought, lay by for a rainy day. I do. not proposse to place before your readers a long array of figures; it is sufficient for my pur- pose to draw your readers' attention to the exist- ence of such friendly .societies as the Oddfellows,l the Foresters, the Druids, Gmkieners, W.A.'s. As a Past Provincial Grand ll:aster of the Warrington District of Oddfellows, and also as one who has always taken an Active part in the details of the so- ciety, many cases come under my notice wherein great good would ensue to the general public were it possible for the§e societies to work more in sym- pathy with the Board of Guardians. What I have to sity of my own society can equally be said of each one of the other societies, but it is of my own I propose to speak. In each district ' exists what may be called• a branch society, which for' distinctive purposes is called the Widow and Orphans Fund. Membership to this fund, by members of the Order, is optional. Contributions are almost nominal, yet in the War- rington District alone the funds now reach the sum of .£7OO. Four times a year delegates meet and consider applications, and in this way scores of poor widows and numbers of destitute orphans receive timely help. As a delegate, the pre- sent writer has just attended.theluarterly meeting of the members of this fund. The number of applica- tions were four. I propose to slightly sketch them. - The first . case was that of widow AI, far advanced in years, and altog6ther too decrepid to earn her own livelihood. She resides with her married daughter, the husband

of whom, a steady man, has not for a long number of months been able to earn stlfacient for their vi''ants. Of sons there are several, some soher and hard working, and one 3r two, I am sorry to say, lazy and drunken. To this widow, under cer'zain

- wise conditions, .E 5 was granted. Second case, the widow works at the factory; her aged father, superannuated member of the Order, receives 2s. 6d. per week. With this, and what the widow can earn, they manttge to keep off the rates, and keep a home together. .£5 was granted. Third case; Mr. Editor, I should like some of those fine folks who are fond of abusing working-men, and calling them thriftless, to have heard this case stated. It was that of an orphan' ; father and mother dead. The child bad been sent to the workhouse; from thence it had been taken and adopted by a young married couple, nothing related. Ilard times, no work, altogether te:d their tale, and application on the child's behalf was made. In thie case school fees had been pressed for. I might cover a column with sentiment on this case. Perhaps your readers can guess it all, and excuse me. Sutlide it to say that again the grant of £5 was male, and I hope the society will see its way clear to relieving the ratepayers of the enormous burden of paying this orphan child's school fees. Fourth case. This., sir, differs from the last, as, unfortu- nately there is a mother in the way. It is pitiful to have it to say, but the mother with her child would have received help and sympathy from the Order to which her husband belouged. but the mother's character gone no help was due to her, and, the, pity of ft, the child suffers in consequeuce4 Yet help will be given—the child will be looked after. Is there no way of removing the evil influence surrounding this child's life? Are the resohrces of civilisation" ap- plicable only to tbe political world? Daring the past 20 years I have seen scores of these casescand I have often asked myself the question, " To what does it all point ?" Numbers of cases have I seen where the Guardians, entirely oblivious to the good •these societies are doing, have demanded their pound of flesh. Tradesmen and manufac- turers never acknowledge the material benefits they receive, through the, rates being lightened, be sending a handsome subscription. No. they prefer to' do it another way; allow me to sketch it. For a long, long period trade has been de- pressed; working-men once in good positions see their hoosehdid goods go one by one: They see trade returns showing an increase in exports, think it over a little, and come to one and the only conclasion, that machinery and not men is now doing the work. The largest firm in War- rington can turn out three times more, work now than it. could ten Years ago, and with half the number of hinds. Reasoning this way; they come across Socialist literature, drink In the most, objectionable teachings of Socialism, meet in Trafalgar-square or at New Crass, Manchrstet4. Papers appear next morning containing reports of serious riots; ef shops being broken into, and club windows smashed. This stirs the gentry up; the Lord Mayor Marts a Mansion Howe Fund.. The provincial, gentry follow suit, and having done all this they go quietly home, and think they have settled the business. In Warringten the Mayor called a meeting, the most noticeable feature of which was that ladies end gentlemen not at all connected with the industries of the district at- tended, and those whose fortunes had been created in the mill and the forge remained away, " snug in their country ' homes. A society called the "Charity Orgaoisation Society" 'was started. What it is going to do I don't know; I am afraid none of its members know. To my knowledge ode application has been made. It has met, no far, with no response, although the cise is pitiful. From a conversation I have had, it seems the case is not bad enough because the people happen to own some furniture. It is not bed enough, although the poor mat*, working in the factory, has worked and starved, until her Cshopinates have divided their day's fold with her. Why. the ladies and gentlemen who are members of this society ought to hide their very hauls for shame. What do they give out of their thousands, in comparison with the working- man's gifts? Of one working-man's society I could tell et each year seeing near upon a Hundred pounds being given away. A mile et red tape must be cut before the more res- pectable and more fashionable society will give away even £5.

SHOOTING A WIFE—On Surdav anion nand John Byrne, a retired sergeant of the Royal Irish constabulary, living in Little Britain-street, Dublin, shot his wife, Cathe- rine Byrne, with a revolver. Byrne was discharged a year ago suffering from melancholy. He left his f unity in Octo- ber. About a week since he wrote to ask his wife to meet , him at Phoenix Park, but he failed to keep the appointment. On Sunday night he went to her house and called her out, and then fired four shots from a revolver at her, one of which lodged in the abdomen. She is not expected to re- cover. Byrne is new under remand. THE NO-RENT CANIPSIGN.—The rents Olathe Kilinore estates have been collected under the "plan of campaign." by two members of Parliament. It is stated that Archbishop Walsh is boycotted because h/has given in his adhesion to the "plan of campaign." A large number of Roman Catholic upper classes of Dublin refuse to dine at his Grace's table, or meet him elsewhere. A remarkable incident in connec- tion with the "plan of campaign" is reported from near Lie. towel. About 300 persone, with a number of horses and carts, assembled OR Saturday on the farm of a usia named Fitzmaurice, of Lixnard. near Listowel, and practic illy car- ried out the plan by removing all his stock and implements to another farm in order to avoid seizure for rent. RUNAWAY HOUSES: SHIUMIS ACCIDENT.—!bout two o'clock en Saturday afternoon an accident of a serious nature occurred at St. Helens. Mr. J. G. Fletcher, cab proprietor and undertaker, Bickerstaffe-street, having several funerals to conduct, arranged with another local undertaker for the supply of horses for a mourning coach. Two young horses were sent in charge of George Cotes- worth, of Wilfrid-street, who proceeded to harness them to one of Mr. Fletcher's mourning coaches. Whilst doing so, ens of the animals reared, and although William Rogiison, clerk to Mr. Fletcher, went to its head and tried to pacify it. his efforts were unsuccessful. Both animals bolted, knocking Cotesworth down and running over him, and vio- lently forcing Rogerson away. They then bolted at great speed along Hall-street and into Church-street, where Mrs. Kirkham, of Grace's-row, Batton, was knocked down, and the horses dashed against the wall of the Van Tromp Inn. The pole and springs of the vehicle were broken, and the box and back torn off—in fact, the coach was almost corn- pletelv wrecked, and it will cost about £1.5 or £2O to repair Cotesworth and Mrs. Kirkham were assisted to Dr. Gas- kell's surgery, where they were attended by Dr. Greig (as- sistant), and afterwards taken home. LIFEBOAT DISASTIIIIFt7ND.—A meeting of the committee of the Lifeboat Disaster Fund was held at touthport on Thursday, the Earl of Derby in the chair. It was decided to grant an allowance of 15s a wee tt to each widow and 51 to each child up to the age of 16 years (this absorbing about £21,000), to grant 155 a week to the survivors of the South- port crew, and to purchase a fishing bolt for each of them, and to make grants to the local committees for the erection of monuments. It was stated to be very doubtful whether there would be any surplus. Smprisra DISASTERS.—The French trawler Josephine, which gained notoriety through b 2ing towed into Lowestoft by the cruiser Ariel, has, it is believed, been lost with all hands. The vessel left Ostend on December 2nd, and has not since been heard of. The steamer Dragoman, which left Liverpool for Cardiff on Saturday, when off Bardsey Istact.; about three o'clock on Sunday morning, collided with a ves- sel bound from London in ballot for Maryport. causing her to sink in a few minutes. The ciptain and four men were rescued by the Drageman, which returned with them to Liverpool, but 14 of the crew were drowned. The Drago- man was very much damaged eft. The name of the vessel lost was the Duke of Connaucnt, a four-masted ship. The steamer's boat cruised about for an hoar among the wreck- age of the sunken ship, but faiied to find any other survi- vors. The Dragoman had her b3w stove in, and suffered other serious injury. The Peninsular and Oriental Gml- PacY's steamer from Tasmania arrived in Plymouth Sound on Sunday, with the captains and crews of no fewer than seven wrecked and abandoned vessels.

div.p: EMMANUEL CHURCH OA. PARTY AND
ENTERTAINMENT.

On Tuesday, the annual tea meeting and enter- tainment in connection with Emmanuel Church was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, the hall having been very effectively decorated with Scriptural mottoes, evergreens, and trophies of flags, by Mrs. O'Brien. About 500 persons at down to an excell- ent tea; tables being giVert,or presided over by the following :—Miss Tetloiv, Mrs. Howard, Miss Sutton, Mr. Milling, Mrs. Gandy, 'Mrs. T. Allen, Mrs. W. Allen, Mrs. Lees, WI T. Woods, Mrs. Birchall, Mrs. Page, Mrs. liesketh, Mrs. O'Brien, Mrs. Parsons, Mrs Landon, Miss Hindley, and Mrs. Spinks. After tea the hall was cleared and the entertainment 'was given. The chair was taken by Mr. R. A. Naylor,who in the course of an introductory address said that I on the previous day he had received -from a great I man—he called him a great man hecaute he was a great man, at any rate in this country—a very beautiful New Year's card, and on that card was a quotation from Lord Bacon to this effect, " It' is heaven upon earth to have a man's mind move in charity, rest in Providence, and turn upon the poles of truth." Now if they wanted to have any real, i genuine happiness, pleasure, and satisfaction n the year 1887 they could only succeed' in obtaining it by permitting their hearts to be filled with that charity. (Hear, hear.) He did not know whether his position there that night was a consistent one or,not, but'upOn religious iiWters he certainly had a great amount of charity for those who did not happen to see eye to eye with hipa upon all the various details of religious life. He was under the impression that if a High Churchman had infited him to be present to take the chair it wouldlave given him just the same amount of pleasure as it did to preside for the Reformed Church of England, because from vhat he found in moving amongst High Churchmen, Low Churchmen, and Bkoad Chnrchmen, in going lip and down the coun- try, and amongst the various denominations, he had come ,to the .conclusion' 'that they had a lot, of genuine and Christian men belong- ing to the various religious sections they found in existence at that moment. The Church, he regretted to say, Was split up into sections, and I they were something' like cats and dogs quarrelling with each other. What they,wanted was the vari- ous sections cemented. together; they 'could not afford te Itave any gutirrelling_. th the present mo- ment, when infidelity, socialism, and communism were spreading abroad at a very rapid rate. It be- hoved all good, true, and faitlif4l Christians of ,the present generation not to have words of discord with one another, but rather to join hand in hand, =Mean in heart, and be determined that in the , strength of Omnipotence they would do what they possibly could to stem the torrent of iniquity which was spreading over this laud at the present moment. (Hear, hear.) He had been glad to see from several letters from ex-presidents of the Wesleyan Confer- ence that they were holding out the olive branch to the New Connexion, and he asked could not the principle be extended a little bit farther? Why sheuld not the Church of England hold out the same inducement to the Wesleyans and other re- ligious bodies to come over the line, and join in one grand united whole? (Hear. hear.) And, further than that, they were going this year to dis- play their loyal generosity by celebrating the Jubilee of her Majesty's reign. (Ap- plause.) He ;Ares glad to see that there were loyal- hearted people present. It was a grand thing tO hon Our the Queen. Her Majesty ' was spoken ill of by some people, and unjustly so, for they had the best Queen in this country than any nation in the past had been favoured with. (applause). All loyal and true-hearted Englishman were prepared to make some little sacrifice to do honour to her Majesty, and he asked why they shotild not act upon the same principle in religious matters, (Hear, hear.) What a grand celebration of the Queen's Jubilee it would be if the Churches and Church clergy of Warrington were to try to make some concession to their friends, the members of the Reformed Chureh I They wanted more unity and less bickering, and he hoped they wbuld endeavour to display the beautiful spirit of Christian love in their relations to their fellow creatures. (Applause.) Why should they be any longer at loggerheads one with another? Let them have genuine sentiments, and let them have a general hand-shaking all round. (Hear, hear.) Let them act on the give- and-take system of Chiistianitv, then there would be brought about a reconciliation, when one denom- ination would join with another, and then the source of weakness which was at present mani- fested would begin to be mitigated. (Applause.) —The musical part of the programme was then proceeded with, and consisted as follows:—" Love's request," Mr. Ikin " I dreani'd a dream," Miss Nixon; violin solo, Mr. G. Shakeshaft ; "Be true to me," Miss Paul; "The longest way round," Mr, Grounds; "The better land," Miss Heaton; duet. "Sweet be her dream," Miss Nixon and Mr. Grounds; comic song, Master W. Bellian •, "The maid of the Mill," Mr. Ikin; violin solo, Mr. G. Shakeshaft ; "Ever of thee," Miss Horton; "Robin dair," Miss Paul; "The old lock," Miss Nixon ; duet, "The giPsY countess," Miss Paul and Mr. Grounds. All the above items were very happily rendered, the per- formances on the 'violin by Mr. Shakeshaft, and the comic songs by Mr. Bellian, being in particular warmly appreciated. The choir also sang several glees in an excellent manner. Mr. G. Riley efficient- ly accompanied on the piano. In •conclusion, Mr. Woods proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies and others for their services in connection with the gathering. The Rev. W. Bibby, in seconding, stated that he was afraid that his connection with Em- manuel Church was shortly to terminate. As many of those present might know, a resident minister had been appointed, and he hoped they would re-.

Ifully re tlise that, .though they have some cause for shouting, they are not yet &ft of the wood. They have still a lion in their path in the shape of Lord RANDOLPH CFIURCHILL —a lien that will be all the more intractable when he perceives that provision is being made for the new-corner to poach on what he looks upon as his own hunting giound. The leader of the Tdry Democrats could forgive the Government, if they would not make peace with him, for putting a weak man in his place; it would be so easy at any time to push him aside; but, if report speaks trulvt-, he is wrathful at the prospect of having to try conclusions with a strong man like Mr. GOSCHEN, when he is disposed to retain to the fold. Lord SALISBURY is, to be sure, more than justified in carrying on the Gov- ernment without Lord R. CHURCHILL—if he can ; but whether he can or not remains to be seen, The Tories are as a rule wonder- luny docile in taking orders from their re- cognised leaders, after they have °ace re- lieved themselves as Englishmen by grumbl- ing, and it is just possible that they may close their ranks and leave their late leader in the House of Commons without a following in Parliament. But his supporters outside the charmed circle at St. Stephens are legion. fie represents the new school of thought anion& the Tories—the school of young men who are a little wider awake than their fathers. They are a stage, and a stage only, behind the Liberals, and it is Lord RAN- DOLPH'S opportunity that they are taking the place of the old-fashioned Tories tvho are slowly but surely becoming extinct. They will constitute the backbone .of the Tory party of the future, and, as Lord RAN- DOLPH CHURCHILL is their leader, he is not Rut rid of when a Cabinet is constituted with- ont him.

With regard to the Liberal Unionists, some of them seem to think they can continue to hold the balance of power; but they may find themselves before long on the horns of a dilemma. Mr. GOSCHEIsi may have no scruple about supporting a Local Government Bill which is framed to represent the classes rather than the masses. He has persistently and con- sistently opposed the extension of the Iran- chisei and it will be in the nature of things with him to take care that the franchise is not all powerful in county government. But Lord HARTINGTON and the rest of the Liberal Unionists stand on different ground; they cannot possibly support a measure which is too narrow for Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL; so that the Government may be said to be doomed the moment it attempts to legislate. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN sees this, and would seem disposed to cut the connection. As soon as, he knew Lord RANDOLPH had resigned he made overtures to his old friends in a speech at Birmingham. "Is it not possible," he asked, "now once more that we may make an honest attempt, if not to agree upon every point, at least to agree upon this, that we will proceed to carry out all those important re- forms upon which there is no difference, and that we will leave it to time, and free and frank discussion, to say YVhethcr, N:Yheri ice have accomplished all these, we shall not go one j (Oiler jrl the direction of those who unfortunately are now opponents." The result of this " feeler " was to draw Mr. JOHN MORLEY to his side, and this meeting of the two leaders has been followed by a proposal for a Conference between Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Sir GEORGE TREVELEYAN on the orte, side, and Mr. MOBLEY and Sir WILLIAM HARCotat on the other, with Lord HERSCHELL as a sort of judicial "go- between." We are not about to assume that this Conference will be the means of settling all the differences of the Liberal party; but it is indicative of a better feeling amongst Liberal 'Unionists, and also of profound dis- trust of the Tories amongst the Radical sec- tion of the Unionists. The reconstructed Government may drag on for a time, and we sincerely hcpe it will not go to pieces just yet. If Mr. GOSCHEN should succeed in keeping the Ministry together until all who call themselves Liberals find a common basis of action, he will have rendered a service such as he little dreams of, and we shall ever have occasion to be grateful to him for the way in which he went over to the enemy.

"The Financial Reform Almanack for 1887" has just been issued; and, as it is edited with customary care, it is a matter of course to say that it is a magazine of arms for the politician who is in earnest in the endeavour to do something to leave the world better than he found it. As the first object of the Financial Reform Association is to induce the most rigid economy in the expen- diture of public money, the news that a Tory Chancellor of the Exchequer has re- signed rather than make himself responsible for estimates that he cannot defend, will have proved "as welcome as flowers in May:" An attempt is being made to discount Wore- hand the explanation which Lord RXt4DoLPH CHURCHILL will make as soon as Parliament meets. It is being suggested that he has no case because the estimates for the Army and Navy are not largely increased; but let those who thin superficially consider the matter turn to the pages of the " FinanciA,l Reform Almanack," and if they are not either blind or stupid they will inevitably come to the concltsion that, for a time of peace, our national expenditure is inflated and abnormal. To confine ourselves for a moment to the cost of the Army and Navy, we find on turning to page 77 that ten years ago—that it in 1876—the total cost was, roundly speaking, £26,000,000 ; but for 1886 it was no less than £39,000,00e. Allowing that this included a special vote of credit for £9,000,000 last year, during the expectation of war with Russia, it will still be seen that there is'an increase in the ordinary estimates for.the Army and Navy of £4,000.,060. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in deal- ing with the requirements of the ensuing year. is bound, if he itloes his duty conscientiously, to take hito account the £9,000,000 thrown into the lap of the War Department last year; and it is little enough, under the circumstances, to take steps, as it is understood Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL proposed to do, to effect. a sub- stantial reduction, We are at peace, and likely to remain at peace, if we cm be con- 'tent to mind our own business, and yet we have an income tax at the high figure of eightpence in the pound—just as if we were in the midst of a great war. Going back as to this matter, too, for ten years, we are re- minded that in 1876 the income tax "as twopence in the pound that is jusc one fourth of what is being levied to-day. Is this high figure re- asonable ? Is it required in the interest either of the army and navy, or of the coun- try? Tne income tax, let it be borne in mind, is a war tax, and is levied as such upon a special class. Twelve millions have dur- ing the past year been squeezed out of this class, and that, too, whilst the nation is at

peace; and the question naturally arises— What may we expect to be called upon to pay in time of war? The tax ought to be re- duced forthwith ; and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL deserves the thanks of all true Reformers for having in this matter of finance' shown the courage of his convictions. He in turn will, we dare say, be disposed to thank the conductors of the 'Financial Reform Al- manack " for the admirable ' way in which they have educated him on this important question of national expenditure. 1

A Boy BURNED AT W'inSEs —a. young lad named Thos. Bather, the Adopted son of Mrs. Hatton, of Sicum's Cross, has been severely burned about the thighs and arms, owing to an apron which be had os at the time becoming ignited while be was lifting a kettle off the kitchen fire. He TM conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where he is now pro- greasing favourably. . AGED PERSONS TREAT AT RUNC.DEN.—AS will be seen from our advertisement columns, the Committee of the Young Men'd Christidn Association have made arrangements for the annual treat to be tritest to persons aged over 60 in the town. A capital tea will be provided, and afterwards lan excellent entertainment will be 'giVen; and the affair II promises to be as successful as in former years.' ' A BF.GOAR AND 1119 LETTERS AT Wins,—At Widnes 'Police Court, on Tuesdsv, before Mr.G.Pilkington, Edward Coyle, a tramp, was charged with begging. P.C. Messen- ger proved that on that morning the prisoner was begging from house to house in Deacon road. At one place he re- ceived a pair of shoes. The constable searched the prisoner, and found upon him 43 begging letters and 7d in capper. The magistrate sentenced the pritioner to a fortnight's hard labour.

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY ComanTrait.-3 meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon., The suggested rules of the Library were under consideration;aud one that all persons employed or resi- dent in the town should be entitled to borrow books, objec- tion was taken to persons working in Widnes, but living in Runcorn, having that privilege. The subject was ad. journed. The chairman stated that the library, would not ' probably be opened until March. ' A GUILTY THIEF AT WIDNES.—A young man named Richard Rawlinson, of no fixed residence, was charged with having, on•ths 18th nit, stolen a pair of boots, worth 3s 3d, from the shop of Thomas Hall, boot and shoe manufacturer, Waterloo-road. The boots were hung outside the shop door on the morning of the day named, and in the evening they were missed. Two days later the prisoner got a girl named Jones, who lives in Oxford-etreet, to pledge the boots for him. When apprehended by P.C. Thompson the prisoner admitted his guilt. He was remanded for a week. • STRANGE Duent AT RUNCORN.—TO-day an inquest is to . .

be held upon the body of a man unknown, apparently about 50 years of age, Lie entered the town about a week aeo, and took up his quarters at the common lodging house of Phillips in Fryer-street, and described himself as a machine mender. On Thursday night he went.. to bed about eleven

o'clock, and at once hecat-ne ill. Phillips undressed the man, and left him, and although he subsequently heard him moaning and praying at 12.30, did not see him again. Yesterday morning the man was found lying on the room door dead. _ _ _

A DRUNKEN WOMAN'S DITCHING AT RUNCORN.—At Ran. corn Petty Sessions, on Monday morning, Mary Spencer, a young woman of bad character, Was charged with being drutik in Percival's-lane, on the 7th December. On the night of that date P.C. Hammersley heard screams in the direction of the canal, and proceeding there he found the defendant in one of the locks. A boatman threw her a rope and got her out. She was very drunk, and the constable took her hotne.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and said she caught her foot against something, and fell into the water . Superintendent Hollingsworth said the defendant had been before the Bench on numerous occasions.—Defendant: I hope you will put a fine on me, sir. (Lauebter, in which the defendant joined•)—A gee of 55 and costs, 9s 61, or seven days' bard labour, was 1113p080(1. DEATH AND FUNERAL ON A WIDNES WESLEYAN. At the pitriirehial age of 73 years, Mr. C. Brown' oae of the oldest %corkers in the Wesleyan cause in Widoes. and an cinder manager at the works of the Widnes Foundry Coni- piny, died last Friday night. As an engineer Mr. Brown bad won a considerable reputation. Trained at the Haigh Foundry, near Wigan, under his own father, he subsequently was manager at works in Wigan, Rainhill, and Liverpool, and 15 years ago he took up hie peeitleil at the Widnes foundry, where his advice On all points of skill was care- fully listened to. He had held almost all the lay offices in the Widnes Wesleyan circuit, Tee fuceral took place on Tuesday at Farnworth Church, the body being followed to the grave by about 200 friends and foundry employers. IBefore the cortege proceeded to Farnworth a service was held at Victoriawoad Chapel, where the Rev. J Eardon' pronounced a short oration. MILK ANALYSIS: A Runconee CAsm.—Joseph Derbyshire, a retail dealer in milk in a small way, appeared before Cap- tain C. W. Hazlehurst and Mr. A. Thomes, at Runcorn 'Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of selling a Dint of milk, which was not of the "nature, substance, and quality" demanded. On the 11th December a constable purchased the milk /rem the defendant, and subsequently a portion wae forwa,ededto tbecounty analyst (Dr. Cat ter Hell) for his report. Superintendent Hollingswoe, en now put in a certificate front the analyst, who staled the milk was add- terated with 12 per cent. of 'enter. During a conversation between the Bench and the Superintendent it transpired that after receiving the sample the analyst requested that a portion of milk should be Obtained from the cows on the farm where the defendaut alleged he had pnrchaeed his. Accordingly a constable etas despatched to the farm ef Mr. Stokes, at Rocksavagre On the 17th December. tie taw the cows milked, and then took a portion from the liquid when all had been mikta together. This was forwarded to the analyst, who afterwards made his report.--Captain Hazle- harat maid the certificate submitted showed there was a dif- ference of t."l per cent of water between the two samples, and the Bench refused to convict upon it. Why was not the comparison made between the sample, and the lowest stan- dard of milk allowed by law.—On the application of Super- intendent Hollingsworth the case was adjourned for a week it order to ascertain if the analyst could give an amended tertificete. CHARGE AGAINST 1 RIINC3II/4 PUBLICA.I7.—A Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday before Captain C. W. Hazleburet and Mr. A Thomas. Joseph Oates, landlord of the Fleetwood Arms. Church-street, was summoned for sell- ing intoxicating liquor to two drunken persons. Mr. W. H. Linaker, defended.—P.S. Blair deposed that on Christmas Eve, about half pat ten he saw two men named Morgan and O'Neil who were very drunk, go into the Fleetwood Arms. He waited a qaarter of an hour thinking they would be turned out but as they were not he entered the house ac- companied by Constable Povey and Sutton. In a part of the vaults that was boarded from the remainder he found the two mall each with a glass of Porter before him. He called the landlady's attention to the men, and she took a glass of porter away to another part of the 'vaults and stated it belonged to another man. Outside O'Neil said "you might have let us drink that glass. It was mine; I paid for it." In reply to Mr. Linaker, the witness said the men were stag- gering about the street before they went in.—P.C. Sutton corroborated. Mr. Linaker for the defence, said Mrs. Oates gave a direct denial to the charge. Mrs. Oates had knot the house for the past 13 years and during that time there had not been a complaint made about the house. He argued that at a busy time like Christmas Eve it was quite possible for a drunken man to get to the counter without being ob- served, and ask for liquor in a clear manner because many a man was drunk in his legs when he was not drunk in his tongue. Mrs. Ann Price said she was employed at the Fleetwoed Arms on Christmas nye and saw the men come in. They were not drunk.—Thomas Saunders, son of Mrs. Oates, also deposed to seeing the men come in. A person that was in asked Morgan what he would have, and they each had a porter. O'Neil went to another part of the house to talk to some woman and had nothing to drink in the house. The men talked quietly to their friends, and in hie opinion the men were not drunk.—Mrs. Oates stated that the men were not drunk, and had Morgan asked for three or four glasses she would have served him as she theught he WAR qualified to take it —Captain Ilielehurst said there was A doubt in the case and they would give the defendant the benefit of it by dismissing the case.—Superintendant Holl- ingsworth thereupon withdrew the charges of drunkenness

against the men. FREE LIBRARIES AND THE JUBILEE.—" Truth" says: "The good people of Luton appear to have hit upon as sensible a method as any I have yet seen of celebrating the Jubilee. Their proposal is to adopt the Free Libraries, Act, and found a public library and science and art classes. A similar memo- rial in every town in England might do at least as much for the Empire as an Institute at South Kensington." ANOTHER OUTBREAK OF HYDROPHOBIA. IN CHESHIRE.—There seems to be a disposition tin official quarters to extend the provisions of the Con- tagious Diseases Animals Act, which are much more stringent than the. Dogs Act, rendering offenders liable to a penalty of £2O, to all divisions of the county. A special meeting of the magistrates was held at Altrincham on Thursday afternoon to con- sider a statement of the Chief Constable with res- pect to hydrophobia. at Dunham Massey. An order under the Dogs Act expired at the end of November, and considerable feeling existed against a renewal. - At the meeting considerable difference of opinion prevailed. Amongst the magistrates assembled some were for contracting the area, others for the whole division, while one or two objected in tote. Ultimately, it is stated, the meeting broke up in confusion without any decision being arrived at.

THE LATCHFORD ELOPEMENT CA.SE.—At Bunts- ford Sessions, on Thursday, James Woodcock, the prisoner in the Latchford elopement case, was sen- tenced to four months' imprisonment. Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., at the last election 1 as the Gladstonian candidate. PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—On Wednesday evening a meeting of the association was held in the Wesleyan School- , room, when Miss Pfsker read an 'able and interes- ting paper on "Metmerism." , There was a good at- I tendomce. At the close an animated discussion took i place, in which the following members took part— Messrs. R. Garnett, C. E. Parker, Davison, R. E. Gar- I nett, John G. Gornall, Manley, A. I. White, Mrs. , Garnett, and Mrs. C. E. Parker. A hearty vote ofl thankS was afterwards accorded to Miss Parker. Mr. 'Jame g Watson occupied the chair. • STIDIOEN DEATH IN A. RAILWAY CARRIAGE. A sudden death -occurred at Newton Bridge Station-on • Thursday night. A train, supposed 'to contain no t passengers, arrived at Huyton Quarry, and in a 1 third-class compartment 'was found an elderly , woman in an unconsclouS state. ,he was taken to I the waiting-roomnnd a doctor summoned, btit be- , fore his arrival life was extinct. From the ticket I found upon her communication was made with I Huron Quarry, the result being that the body was claimed by the husband, Mr. Mercer, market gar- , dener. The deceased had been to Liverpool on • business said was taken suddenly ill on the Why home.

TEA PARTY AND WATCHNIGHT.—The Wesleyan Methodists of Penketh, according to custom, held a tea party on New Year's Eve in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. Tea was on the tables at 7 p.m., when there was a very good attendance. The tea party was held as a preliminary to the watchnight. After the tables were cleared, a meeting was held, at which Mr. Garnett presided and delivered a stirring address. Bertie Cook recited the "Roll call," R. E. Garnett recited "Pit and his pendulum." and Miss Mabel Garnett "The healing of Janus' daughter."' Songs were sung by Miss Garnett, and addresses were delivered by Itessrs. R. Cook, Watson, Kilken, and Chester, At 10-30 the watchnight was com- menced, the Rev. J. Howell Jones conducting the , service. He preached an excellent sermon from thei 90th Psalm, 12th verse, "So teach us to number our days that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." There was a large company present, and the service ended with singing the well-known tune, "Come let us anew our journey pursue."

ANOTHER WAD-FORMING COMPETITION. - En- couraged by the success achieved in their former competition,,Messrs. Crostield and Sons, as will be seen from our advertising columns, have announced that they will hold another word-forming competi- tion. The coming competition, however, is on a very much larger scale than the preceding one, no less than £lBO being offered in prizes, and out of this the fortunate winner of the first prize will re- ceive the handsome sum of £4O. The second prize is £2O, the third £lO, fourth £5, fifth £3, sixth .e 2. and there will also be twenty-five £1 prizes. £5 will likewise be given for the best list from Eng- land, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, and a similar amount for the best list trom abroad. Some hand- some prizes will also be given for the nearest guess to number of entries in the competition. It will be seen, therefore, that plenty of 13COD0 is given for the exercise of judgment and ingenuity on the part of the competitors. In the word-forming competi- tion the words are to be formed out of Crosfield's Llamas," these words having been suggested by the fact that Messrs. Crodeld and Sons have secured the foar llamas which were to be seen in the Indian Village at the recent Liverpool Exhibition, and whidh are now making a tour of the provinces yoked to a specially made carriage and attended by natives.

Diplomatic pressu,re is being puton Turkey in consequence of her being just now hand and glove with Russia; but the talk about going to war and bombarding Constantinople is just So much nonsense.
Lord Salisbury has re 6onstructed his Cabinet, but who will say that it is stronger? He has lost Lord Randolph Churchill and Lord Iddesleigh, and gained—Mr. Goschen !
Randy Horner sat in a corner Spoiling the Cabinet Pie; He put in his thumb and pulled out a plum, And §ai4—" What 0, bad boy am I,'

• Speaking a tßuncorn, on Wednesday even- ing, Lord Dunraven said he would venture to stake his head that Lord R. Churchill would be with the Goveanment on the Irish question. Perhaps; but what is the stake worth? If he had "gone the whOle animal" and offered to stake "a pony," he might have found someone to take him. But stake or no stake, "we shall see what we shall see."
The new leader of the Tories is to be "a party of the name of Smith. Umph I One has heard the name before." And this, ac- cording to "Punch," is ‘• how it came about „
Our Randolph we've lost, and we cannot get Harty— A Leader we must have with power and pith; Well, it seems to need welding, the Unionist Party; One might have a worse than a Smith!

Mr. Goschen has been wandering in the wilderness for thirteen years, for it is that length of time since he figured as a member of a Government. However,'as Tory Chan. cellor of the Exchequer, he has reached the Promised Land. He sees things now from a new point of view, for he makes his patriotism pay. I wouldn't give Salisbury and Co. a blank cheque, Said Goschen with lip on the sneer; Just so; he prefers to receive one, filled up— A cheque for five thousand a year.

Lord Salisbury, of ccurse, loves Mr. Gos- chen; he always did, and this is what he said of him on the 4th November, 1885 "Without in the least wishing to rob the Liberal party of the treasures they possess, I only hope that when they have a great deci- sion to take they may be compelled to rely on Lord Derby, and when they have an unpopu- lar opinion to support by vote as well as by speech they may be compelled to rely upon Mr. Goschen,"

The Town Clock a7—W—arrington couldn't be "on the strike" when it stopped at Christ- mas Eve; and it was not because it was too "elevated," as some have hinted. It suffered rather from wafer on the brain. It was rain, followed by rust, which brought the clock to its brief standstill.

"Feed my lambs" was the motto upon which Mr. J. B. Leach and other friends acted, at St. Helens, on New Year's Day. Over 1,000 youngsters—the poorest of the poor—were supplied with food both for body and mind; and did'nt they enjoy the combination of plum cake and conjuring—rather !

Mary Spencer, of Runcorn, has had a nar- row escape. She got tipsy, and fell into the canal, but was hauled out. If she had con- fined herself to water in the first instance, she would not have fallen into water in the second. She would do well to mend her ways; there may not always be a man and a rope handy.

Councillor Biker has elicited the,informa- tion that the Warrington Corporation has no pt:Oret to spend the ratepayers' money in erecting a Cabman's Shelter. But has the Matter to rest there? Is there no other way of "raising the wind." Not, by-the-by, that it needs raising; it is enough to take one's hair off sometimes. And it is so cold, too: think of it, and let us have the Cabman's Shelter.

A Ragged School for Warrington—that is a good start for the first Sunday in the New Year. All honour to those who have com- menced It. Our best wish is that tie time may come when there will be no netd for such a school; but with 150 scholars on the open- ing day that time will not be yet. Meantime superintendent and teachers must keep " peg- ging away ;" "just as the twig is bent th'e tree 's inclined."

The new Vicat of Runcorn The with a hearty receptiot from his new lastishioner9 on Thursday evening ; and he seems to have been delight ta to find they were not quite such heathens as they have been represented. It touched him to learn that the Nonconform- ists had prayed that God might bless his labors amongst them. There is, therefore, a good feeling all round. Long may it con- tinue.

Town Councillors must not speak disre- spectfully of Warrington gas. It is known to the hundredth part of the reflection of a brass button that its illuminating power is equal to 17 candles and decimal .1.5 over; and, further, that 17 candles and decimal 45 are quite equal to rendering darkness visible—ay, even to the darkness of a black hat, which, as has been proved again and again, is darkness which may be "felt."

--- The Campbell divorce case has borne fruit in the shape of a memorial to the editors of daily papers with a view to the curtailing of unsavoury details in unsavoury cases. It is to be hoped this word to the wise will be sufficient. Editors of daily papers were sad sinners in reporting the Campbell case. Edi- tors of weekly papers were quite saints by comparison; they made a virtue of necessity— they hadn't room to go wrong. The Postmaster-General is the reverse of pleased with the memorial from the St. Helens Town Council to the effect that it was " miclesirahle that her Majesty's Govern- ment should use foreign shipping to carry English mails." The reply which has been received states that "the memorialists have not fully considered the case in all its bear- ings." Possibly not; but they have consi- dered the main issue, and they agree with ninety-nine men out of every hundred in thinking the Postmaster-General has made a mess of it.

It is pleasing to note that there are sips of improved trade for 1887. • A BLEACHING POWDER Coalinga WHACKED AT Win. Ns—An accident of a serious nature occurred at Hutch- inson's chemical works on Saturday afternoon. Owing to some unexplained cause, a number of waggons which were' being shunted in the yard, left the rails and collided with the iron supports of a large bleaching powder chamber. The heavy structure fell to the ground, but happily it was empty, and there was no person in the immediate vicinity at the time, or the consequences to the neighbourhood through the diffusion of a large quanTity of chlorine gas would have been most disastrous; a new chamber will have to be pro- vided, and the cost to the firm will be very heavy. OPENING OF A NEW ORGAN AT DiTTON.—A new American organ, which has been placed in Ditton Wesleyan Chapel, at a cost of £45, was opened on Monday evening. A goodly number of people sat down to a tea, which was provided about half-past five, a largely-attended meeting being afterwards held under the presidency of Mr. Roger Fogg. Addresses were deliveied by Mr. W. Clarke, the Rev. R. Burdon, Mr. S. Stead, and Mr. Joseph Robinson; selections given on the organ by Mr. Skelton, of Mytholm- royd, Yorkshire; and songs rendered by Miss Horton and Mr: A. Fox, of Runcorn. From the report of the organ fund, submitted by Mr. Clarke, it appeared that £53 bed been collected. The balance will be spent In repairing the Instrument when oat of order.

The deceased was employed as a hand on board the Hat Dan, leelongiug te Messrs. Hill and Grundy, of Liverpool. Doe lug the great storm that prevailed on I,he 9th December, the Oat laden with sand W4B coming up the Mersey, and when near the West Lielitshle, the Yeleel Was swamped, The crew, composed of Robert Holdoes of Penketb, his two eons end Wealth, managed to ceramble upon the riggings where they were perceived by the captain of the steamer "Bridge- water."
