CAMDEN WESLEYAN MIIIITAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RITNCORN.—The annual meeting in connection with this society was held on Monday evening in Camden School- room. An extellent tea was provided at five o'clock, to which upwards of 100 members and friends sat down. The chair was afterwards taken by Mr. li. Randle. president of the class, and the election of officers for the ensuing year took place. A vote of thanks was aCCOrdtd to Mr. Randle tor his past services as president, and he was unanimously re-elected. The annual report was read by the secretary and adopted. Mr. J. T. Nickson was re-appointed secretary. Mr. Randle, as the newly-elected president, delivered an address. Addresses were also delivered by the Rev. G. Wood and Mr. S. C. Beckett. A miscellaneous programme of Mule, Aso., was then gone through. The Misses Wood gays a pianoforte duet, "La Furore." Songs were given by 'Miss Jones Miss A. Jones, Mr. W. Millineer, Mr. R. Edwards, mid Mr. John Leathwood. Mr. F. Eden recited Mt. George R. Sims' poem "Ticket o' leave." Concertina solos were given by Mr. T. Wilson, and solos on the whis- tle were contributed by Mr, W. Mill:tiger. A pianoforte solo was also given by Miss A. M. Forster. Miss E. Wright. Miss C. Hampson, and Mr. A. Bibby acted as accompanists. Subsequently the party adjourned to the large schoolroom.' where a variety of social games and pastimes were indulged in until after ten o'clock, Mr. W. I. Shore and Mr. Carroll being the M.C's. The room presented a very pretty appear- ance, much trouble having been spent in the work of decorating.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A fortnightly meeting of this body was held ai. Dutton Workhouse do Tuesday afterroon, under the presidency of Colonel Ashton. There were alto present—The Revs. John Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs. Aaron, Hadfield, Cacapkin, Farrell. Hewitt, Bacaley. H Linaker (clerk), and W. IL Llnaker (deputy clerk.) A letter was read from the suLhorities of Chester Asylum, infor.ning the Board that the cost per head per week for the maintenance of a person in that institution has been reduced to 7s. A letter was read from the assistant overseer for Frodabarn, stating that he had been directed by the senior overseer to say that he was sorry the calls could not be paid this week, and to ask the Board not to take out summonses. The money would certainly be Paid by the nest Board day.— Mr. Aaron remarked that if all the overseers in the union were to do the same as the Overseers of Frodsham and of one or two other places had done, they would not be able to carry on the business of the union at all. It was decided that the Clerk take out summonses at once. The conduct of Mr. Ward relieving officer for

Runcorn, was Complained of by the relations of an old woman who was in receipt of parish relief, and who had had whiskey recommended to her by the Medical Officer of Health for Runcorn. It was stated in their communicatien that Mr. Ward had "gros.sly insulted them,' and as a public servant had treated them most un- HY. He had at first refused to comply with the doctor's recommendation, but afterwards had complied with it.—Mr. Ward explained to the Board what had occurred, and the Board acquitted him of blame.—The Medical Officer of Health for Budwortb wrote informing the Board of his in- tention to resign that position, and recommending to the Board Dr. Argo, who was taking his practise, as a suitable person for the vacancy which would be caused—The re- resignation was accepted.—Dr. Argo also wrote soliciting the office, and enclosing testimonials, and Mr. Aaron gave notice that at the next Board meeting that day month he would move Dr. Argo's appointment. —A letter was read from the Local Government Board requesting the Guardians to furnish them with a medical certificate, showing that Mrs. Jones was unable to perform the duties of matron.— The Clerk said Mrs. Jones was bound to resign when her husband did—Mr. Hadfield: And yet they want to know the reason why she has resigned.—Tne Clerk : It was by their regulations that she had to do so. (Laughter.)—The Board then proceeded to relief business.

A NEWSBOY'S FATAL ADVENTURE AT WIDNES. Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner. held an inquiry at Widnes Felice Court on Monday night, into the circum- stances of the doath of George Hatliwell, 13 years of age, son of a labourer who resides in Catherine-street. Evidence was given by the father, by Frederick Case, cl,rk at the works of Messrs Gossige and Son, and James Tensey, a new4soy. It appeared that Halliwell was a newsboy and on Thursday evening sold an evening paper to Mr. W. W. Go-nage. The boy afterwards discovered that he had given Mr. Gossage a shilling instead of a halfpenny, and went to the office of the firm in order to correct the mistake. Case told the boy that Mr. Goesage had gone away, and that he must come again the next morning. Mr. Thorpe hearing of the matter sent Case to fetch the boy back. Casa went out- side but owing to the for, he could not see the boy although he could hear him crying, and he whistled. Mr. Thorne re- assured the weeping newsboy that if he would come to the office at ha, past nine next morning the matter wonld be pat right; and the boy &touted. As nothing further was heard or seen of the boy, it was surmised that he had got lost in the fog, and probably been drowned; and en Mon- day morning his dead body was found near to the entrance to the canal by his father and Mr. John Die keen junior. ' In reply to questions the witness Case said from the office door of the firm to the river was about 30 yards. The river was unprotected,and deceased walking straight on from the office, if he could not see would walk over a well which was level with the bank and fall a distance of 30 feet into the water below. . The tide was out at the time.—The jury returned a verdict of "accidental death froth drowning," and added a recommendation that a fence or some other protec- tion should be erected at the place in question. As a path- etic incident it may be mentioned that at the treat to News- boy's on the Monday previous. the deceased sang " I such never see my home any more."

NEW YEAR'S DAY AT WIDNES. DRINK AND VIOLENCE. 1887 was heralded at Widnes by the blowing of the whistles and the ringing of the bells at the numerous works, the noise thus produced having great penetrative power if ' not much music. Watch night services were also held at the majority of the churches aud chapels. On New Year's Day work proc•eded as on ordinary occasions, but being Saturday work was supended at noon. Considerable drink- ing of strong liquors took place, and there were numerous scenes of violence, of which the following are those that hal the immediate attention of the police:— At Widnes Police Court, on Moaday, Stephen Scilly, a rough fellow, well known to the police, was charged with having. on Saturday night. assaulted P.C. Holbrook. The officer was walking along Victoria-read, near the Drill Hall, when the prisoner inquired of him why he had locked up his brother. While In conversation the prisoner suddenly struck the officer a violent blow. on the chin with his fist, and also kicked him. In the struggle that ensued, the officer lost his helmet, which bas not yet been recovered. The prisoner, with assistance was locked up, sad be was .now 2entencvd to three months' hard labour—Thomas bcally, labourer, brother to the above-mentioned, was charged with being drunk and oisorderly, and with damag- ing the uniform Of P.C. Holbrook to the extent ofi3s ed. About nine o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner was drank, and wanting to fight another man in Waterloo.road. As the prisoner refused to depart quietly the constable ap- prehended him. On the way to the station the prisoner

- acted with great violence, and tore the officer's coat down the front. The prisoner, who made his 17th appearance, was ordered to pay a total of 2441ir go to gaol 14 days.— Walter Heath, labourer, Oakland-street, was charged with having been drunk and refused to quit the Waist Sank Hotel, kept by Charles McGovan. On Saturday night the prisoner was drunk in the hotel, and having a desire to "spar" with the customers, he was rtquested to leave. He refused, and the aid of Constables Worsfold and Houghton WAS invoked, , and these officers ejected him after a tough straggle. The rprisoner was fined 20a and costs, or a month.—Jaases Ryan, a labourer, of Wslaisley-strect, pleaded guilty to having on &tummy night been drunk at the Adelphi Held, kept by Thomas Ireland, and refused to quit. He also pleaded guilty to damaging P.C. BawerbSak's coat to the extent of 4s. The prisoner was tined ps ana coats on each charge, or in default 14 days' hard labour.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. The annual coneregational tea party •in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, was 'I held in the Mission-room, Runcorn' on Monday night. The room was tastefully decorated, and there was large atten- dance, the parry le.in,e the most suceetsful ever held at the Mission. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Meadow- croft. Mrs. H. White, Mrs. Lake,- Mrs. Merwood, Mrs. 11, Abel, Mrs. Digets, Mrs. Read, and Mies Taylor. After tea the usual entertainment was held, when among the crowded audience were many sailors and flatmen. Dr. McDougall presided, and there were on the platform the Revs. W. Pres- ton, M.A., W. W. K. Ormsby, M.A., Mr. J. Meadowcroft, hon. secretary of the Mission, Mr. William Shaw, and a number of ladies. In an admirable speech, the Chairman mentioned the successful labours of Mr. S. Shaw, the mis- sionary, And gave him the title of the "Boatmen's Bishop.! Alluding to the improvement in the religious, moral, and sanitary condition of the boat people through the passing of the Canal Boats Acts. In Runcorn there were abont.Bso boats registered, which threw upon the local authorities in the way of education great respocsibility ; and schools had been erected chiefly for the accommodation of the children of boat people. It seemed to him that owing to the migra. tory character of boat people advantage had not bent taken of the educational facilities provided to the extent that it ought to have been. It was to be hoped that the boat peo- ple, in their own interests, as well as in the interests of the community generally, would take advantage of those faci- lities for education which had been provided by the School Board. Although the payment of the fees might press un- duly upon some parents, yet they need not be a stambling block in the way of the children's education as power was given for the remission of the fees. He urged the parents to send their children regelarly to school on every occasion which the exigences of their trade permitted. The programme, which was of great diversity, was taken part in by Miss Taylor, Miss Harnpson, Miss Howard, Mies Geodwell; Masters Richard Shaw, Philip Shaw, and F. Mack. Two concertina solos were g;ven by Mr. T. Lunt. Recitations were also given by Mies Martha Holland and MISS Wardle. Short addresses were delivered by the Revs. W. Preston and W. W. K. Ormsby and Mr. Meadowcroft. A Norwegian sailor, named Andrew Christian, also gave an address.—Mr. Shaw proposed that a vote of thanks be givea to the ladies who had presided at the table and who had assisted at the entertainment. He was surrounded, be said, by a band of earnest workers, without whom it would be Impossible to carry on the work of the school.—Mr. Allen seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously.—A. vote of thanks to the Chairman was carried by acclamation on the motion of Mr. Mearlowcroft, seconded by the Rev. W. W. K. Ormsby, and supported by the Rev. W. Preoton. On Tuesday night the annual Christmas tree attracted some 300 children to the Mission-room. They partook of a substantial tea, the.ir wants being attended to by Mrs. Littler, Mrs. Allen, Mrs. Mack, Mrs. Hulme, Miss Owen, Miss Garrett, Miss Bowyer, Miss Toft, Miss Waterworth, Miss Dutton, and Miss Allen. The tree was laden with articles of clothing, besides toys for the children. Up- wards of 300 prizes were distributed, each child receiving lone as a reward for good attendance. The children passed ; a pleasant evening, and at the close gave three cheers for all I who had contributed towards their enjoyment

WELCOME• TO ERE VICAR OF RUNCORN. The Vicar of Runcorn, the R•ev..,... 7•laltiand Wood, M.A., having been inducted into hIS living. the parishioners lost ne tine in giving him a most cordial welcome to his new

sphere of l;boars. The reception took the form of a tea party and entertainment, held in the National Schoolroom on Thursday evening, and the wardens and their co-workers bad some difficulty in providing accommodation at the tea. tables for many hundreds that assembled to partake of the- good things provided. The following ladies presided over- I, the tables :—Mesdames Whittaker, Lake, Abel, Buck, _Da-

...._ .......... ________ , . vies, Gregory. Johnson, Mellor, gatton: Marwood, Be, Croelay, Gorst, G. L. Hulehurst, Imison, Lello, • Moss. Savage, and Jones, and Miss Hampson and Miss Statham. Towards the cost of the tea the following contribu- ted : Messrs. A. Salkeld, S. B. Chadwick, J.P., W. Mellor, Torkington, E. Gregory, Alfred Back, 1 Imison, Statham, Savage, John Davies, M. Barker, W. Sutton, Whittaker, G. Moss. F. A. Lake, E. Marwood, ' G. Bell, J. W. Lightburn, J. N. Lello, Dagdale, and E. A, , Chorlton ; Mesdames Chadwick, Leicester, Gore, Hanle- ' hurst, Brundrit, White, Abel, Johnson, Crosby, Meadow. , croft, and Hampson. At the entertainment subsequently ,I held the infanta' schoolroom was packed to the doors In ' introducing the vicar to the audience, Mr. F. A. Lake, churchwarden, remarked that Mr. Wood, after his remarks on confidence in his sermon on Sunday evening, would not I expect that gushing welcome that an old friend was en- titled to, and be must put it down to that English charac- teristic of not rushing into expressions of endearment ard friendship until there was some satisfactory reason 1 i for doing so. He could not imagine a much more try. lug position for any man than that of a vicar coming into a strange parish, especially where he succeeded one who , had endeared himself so much as their late vicar. (Ap. ' plause.) In an audience like that on such an occasion, the 1 critical faculty must be somewhat active, but they could j exercise it fairly and honestly, and instead of noting every 1 little difference in manner, or the service, or any other peon-- . - . ..

liarity, let them rather endeavour to discover all that was good in each other, so that they could work together ande • help each other. (tapplause.) On behalf Of those present he gave Mr. Wood a hearty welcome and asked him to take • the chair. (Applause.) The Vicar, who was loudly applauded on taking the chair, said although he bad been a clergyman in Cheshire for more than 21. years, he had never been to Runcbrn. As they were unknown to each other, he did not expect to be called upon to succeed one who was so highly respected as Cation Bar- clay was. He had been long enough in Runcorn, however, to think that the town had been greatly maligned. (Ap- plause.) So far as his experience went, it was not a quarter so bad as it was represented. (Applause.) He was most agreeably surprised to find they had such a fine church, and such a fine choir. (Applause.) He advertzd to the Capital work th it appeared to have been done by the lay °Wears of the church and to the kindness they had displayed towards him, and the a3elst ince they bad rendered to him since his arrival. (Applause.) He expressA his gratifies- ticn at the flourishing condition of the school and in a humorous manner urged upon the supporters of the church the completion of the church of St. Michael and All Ange!s.o was much touched by one thing he was told that morning, that in one of the Nonconformist chapels in the town they prayed that God might bless him in his work amongst them. GAS EXPLOSION IN A BA itRACK. NINE LIVES LOST. On Sunday evening a serious explosion occurred at the Cambridge Barrack, Portsmouth, occupied by the Worcestershire Regiment. At nine o'clock, a large meter situated at the rear of the building ex- ploded with a very loud report, destroying a portion . of the building and seriously injuring several men. The sentry on duty at the gate was thrown by the concussion into the toad, and knocked down some passers by. Houses in the vicinity were severely shaken. After the removal of the debris, it was at once ascertained that four men were killed, and that several were buried beneath the ruins. Up to three a.m. on Monday, 19 men had•been removed to the hos- pital. The work of extricating the sufferers pro- ceeded slowly, as the night was dark, and the gas was necessarily cut off from the 'building. The task of digging for the men entombed was resumed on Monday morning. Sir George Willis, the general commanding the district, superintended the operations and ordered inquiries as to the num- ber of men within the block at the time of the acci- dent. It was ftscertained that though the block was occnpied by three companies there were not more than 30 men in occupation, the majority being on leave for Sunday. It is surmised that there was an accumulation of gas under the flooring. but how it became ignited is not known. Nearly all the men who were in the wing were cleaning their kit,so as to be ready for duty on Monday morning; but a few men were sitting round the fire reading. The fall of the ruins was so sudden that most of these were covered by the debris before they could realize their position. The first floor fell almost flat on the ground, but the second floor was propped up at an angle by a dead wall at the back. One man was shot right into the Parade, alighting uninjured on kis feet. Several of the men who were removed to the hospital are in a precarious condition with broken limbs. An inquest was opened at Portsmouth on Tues- day, on the bodies of four soldiers killed by the gas explosion at Cambridge Barracks, on Sunday night. Colonel Watson stated that an escape of gas from the main took place outside the next block, perco- lated through the wall of the damaged block, and on reaching the fireplace ignited. The inquiry was adjourned till Tuesday next.—Private Wilket died on Tuesday night at the hospital, making the fifth death from the explosion. Since then four others have died. The ninth death took place on Thurs- day morning, when Robert William Corlett, riveter, succtimbed to his injuries at the Borough, Hospital, The deceased lived at 2, Brook-place, Birkenhead. The other injured man still in the hospital is Mr. John Allison, superintendent, engineer to Messrs. Smart and.' Co., of London, the owners of the Petriana. An official inquiry was held at the Barracks on Tuesday. Colonel Furze, assistant quarter- master; presided, and the proceedings were con- ducted with closed doors. Several witnesses were axamined.

The gas meter which supplied .the three wrecked barrack rooms has been found to be very defective in the syphon, from which there was a great leak- age, amounting, on the estimate of an officer of the gas company, to Ckft. an hour.. One soldier has stated that he has sometimes had to hang up a blanket round his bed to keep off the fumes of gas, and it is certain that reports respecting the leakage have been made to the RoyalEngMeers' department apparently without effect.
BLUE COAT BROTHERLY SOCIETY.
The thirty-second annual dinner of the Warring-1 ton Brotherly Blue Coat Society took place on Mon-

day evening, at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street,‘War- eington, where an excellent repast was served up. Mr. P. Stubs occupied the chair; the vice-chairs were occupied by Mr. E. Rose and Mr. N. B. Perci- val, and amongst those also present were the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton and S. Wilkinson. Messrs. J. C. Parr, C. White, H. B. White, W. Owen, Nicholson, T. Sutton, T. Moths, J. Davies, T. Robinson, R. Davies, John White, T. Birchen, W. G. Forshaw (hon. sec.), T. Armstrong, A. Dealey, W. Smith, A. Shaw, W. Crank, F. Rose, J. Warburton (Manchester), John Povey, J. A. Short, T. E. Hughes, A. Brimelow, M. Chorley, T. Whittaker, J. Lea, T. Lane, T. S. Burgess, John Burgess, Fred Short, F. Deeley, P. Morris, W. Whittaker, G. Gleave, C. Oldcroft, J. Garnett, T. Rawlinson, T. Pilling, and R. Anderton. Mr. Forshaw, (hon. sec.) reads several letters from gentlemen who were unable to attend. The Rector of Warrington (the Rev. W. Quekett) wrote wishing success to the Blue Coal School; Lord Cross regretted that a previous engagement prevented him from being present; Colonel Blackburne inti- mated that although his absence froth Lancashire would prevent him attending the dinner care would be taken that some days previously some game should be delivered to the assistant sec. for use at it; Mr. James Nicholson, of Thelwall Mall, enclosed £5 towards the Society's funds; and the ex-Mayor (Alderman Harrison) wrote that a severe cold kept him at home. Mr. Forshaw then read the annual report:—"Though nothing requiring special mention has occurred in the work et the Society during the past year, yet it has been on the whole satisfactory. The object of the Society is not only to assist the boys by grants of clothes and money after they leave school, but also to stimulate and encourage them with such advice and sympathy as may be needed, and to ascertain periodically from their employers whether they are satisfied with their conduct and progress. the Committee have exercised the greatest care in considering the ap- plications made to them for clothing and loans; assistance having been only rendered to those whose conduct, both at work and at home, has merited it. (Applause.) The financial position is very satisfactory. The Committee have spent £5l 15s 5d in clothes and grants of money durilig the past year, and, after paying all accounts, there is a balance standing to the society's credit at the Savings' Bank and in the treasurer hands of £5O 9s. Bd. (ipplause.) The balance- sheet, duly audited and printed, will be sent to each of the patrons and members in due course. The committee have every reason to be satisfied with the progress of the society during the year, and also with the result of their labours, and they again desire to express to the patrons their thankfulnessl for the encouragement the society has invariably met with from them, and they. still hope that they may continue to deserve their like confidence and support. The committee, in concluding their re- port, take tl,is opportunity of wishing all present a happy and prosperous new year." (Cheers.) The CHAIRMA.N, in proposing the toast of the "Queen," referred to the Jubilee of Her Majesty's reign. The Queen was, he said, worthy of all the honour which could be proposed and carried out. He trusted that the successful carrying on of the Government of Lord Salisbury, to the benefit of the country, and to the honour of the people and the throne, might be one, and not the least, amongst the many happy events which would be brought about during the year. (Cheers.) The CHAIRMAN also proposed "The Prince and Princess of Wales, and the rest of the Royal Family." Mr. Piing proposed "The Church, the Bishop, and Clergy of the Diocese, and Ministers of all De- nominations," coupling with the toasts the names of the Revs. S. Wilkinson and E. C. E. Carleton. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON responded, and in the course of his sPeech remarked that if, instead of the divisions that now existed between different religions, they might have, as in times past, the parochial and non-parochial clergy working side by I side within the borders of the same church, it would be an improvement upon the present state of things, and the principle of Unity would be maintained. Union was in the air. The various Methodist bodies I were trying to heal their divisions, he believed that the Baptists and Independents were endeavouring to find some basis of union, and he thought that many Churchmen would be glad th hail any pro- posal that would lead to re-union with those separ- ated from the Church, who mtht in the future be united with it. The Rev. S. WILKINSON, who also responded, said that a fp eat deal was in the present day being done to create such a spirit of union as Mr. Carleton had referred to. All were baptised in the name of ' the same Blessed Trinity, fought the same battle agaihst the world, the flesh, and the devil, and, it should be said of them, as was said in ancient times, "See how these Christians love one another." He hoped that something to mark the Jubilee year would be done in eonnection with the Church of England, and that, locally, something might be done in reference to a Jubilee ' Church for St. Peter's parish. Many schemes had been mooted-Mr. Morris had a great one on. hand—but many Churchmen would help in the matter of St. Peters, Which was a subject that had been hanging fire for the last 20 years. (Cheers.) Mr. C. WHITE, in appropriate terms, gave the toast of "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces." Captain NicuoLsois responded to the toast, and referred to the presence of Trumpeter Smith, of the sth Dragoon Guards, and formerly a Blue Coat boy. who now 'wore ,on his breast the Soudan medal. ' (Cheers.) They must, he said, be proud that Trum- peter Smith, an old Blue, should be one of that gallant band of heroes who in Egypt upheld the honour of England. (Cheers.) Trumpeter SMITH also briefly acknowledged the toast. Mr. FORSIIAW, in proposing tbe toast of "The trustees of the school," said that a short time ago Mr. Rose showed him round the school, and he was agreeably surprised to find the comfort and care given to the pupils. He mentioned that to show how properly and wisely the ttusts were being ad- ministered, and to show that the trustees had in Mr. Rose an excellent lieutenant, who was not merely acting as tutor to those committed to his charge, but was redly acting in loco parentis. (Cheers.) It was also pleasing to find that the edu- cation was still being properly maintained, and that through the sYstem which was being encouraged by the trustees such an education was being imparted as would fit the Blues for a useful and honourable career in life. (Cheers.) It was admitted that the institution was one of the most useful in the town, and he would suggest that they could not better commemorate the Jubilee year than by, if possible, extending its usefulness. (Hear, hear.) He was sure nothing would please "Old Blues" better than to see the benevolence of the institution more widely spread. For all the advantages "Old Blues" had derived from the school they were extremely grateful to the trustees, and they, could not better repay them than by endeavouring to become good and eseful citizens, doing their duty in that state of life to Which it bad pleased God to call them. Mr. BrucHALL supported the toast. He said that the Blue Coat School had been of immense benefit Ito Warrington; he hoped that it would be of still I greater benefit. When it was first founded it was almost the only institution that held out its hand to the needy and helpless, and though otherbenevo- lent institutions existed on all hands it still con- tinued to do good and useful work. (Cheers.) The CuAiniuitt responded on behalf of the trus- tees. It had, he said, for a long number of years given him the greatest pleasure to see the way in which the school had been conducted by the mas- ters and mistresses who had been in charge. He hoped that its usefulness would not decrease, and was sure that, under the management of Mr. Rose, it showed no signs of diminution. (Cheers.) Alderman DAVIES also responded, saying that he was proud to be a trustee of the school, and pro- posed the health of the "Chairman," who briefly aeknOwledged the honour. Mr. PERCIVAL proposed "The Mayor and Cor- poration of Warrington." Alderman Surrox, in responding, said that he thought the Corporation of,Warrington did its best for the interests of the town. During the last twenty years rapid strides had been made in the way of improvements, and great progress had been

made. Mr. OWEN OM "Town and trade. and asked sympathy for those who had passed through years of depression—for those who, having in times of prosperity husbanded their resources, had not been able to hold their own for the sake of others whose interest depended upon theirs. He hoped that 1887 would prove more prosperous than its predecessor. (Cheers.) Mr. T. MORRIS, whose name was coupled with the t:oast, referred,to the illness of the Mayor, and said as chief magistrate he gave promises during that, the Jubilee year of Her Majesty, of many things that would directly and indirectly be of lasting

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 8 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 8 1887.

benefit to the people of Warrington, one of these things being the making of the library a free lend- ing one. (Applause.) The time had gone when with impunity they could and did pooh-pooh the German, Belgian, and French products. They must do battle and fight bard to overcome the long time, I less pay, and better education of the working people of the nations named; for unless they did so their staple trade, drawing wire, would grow more lan- guid still—and that need not be, for at times it looked as though it would go spark out from among them. Considering the adverse times tbey had been passing through, and the low prices that had to be taken for goods made, Warrington was in as healthy a state commercially as any town he knew. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Morris pointed out that the German nation paid is 7d per head for each person far edu- cation last year, and England Is 6d, and if England was the rich nation he was said to be, surly she could afford to spend as midi meney as the Germans on the intellect of her people. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They knew that knowledge was power, and if it were they must have know- ledge to enable tbeir men to produce their wares and handicraft, as was the case in Germany. He felt as an Englishfnan for England, but he felt for War- rington in particular. (Applause.) They kept their scholars too long at school; they ought to be made to go to work earlier. The German laws were very similar to their own except in this re- spect. Their English lads, when they left school at 13 or 14 years of age, were bandied about, and if they could not get a cheap book to read they went to the club-room or alehouse, instead of improving their minds. Unless they could improve the minds of their working-men they would have the fellows lie had named at their heels, and even taking the boots cdf their feet; but he felt convinced that if Englishmen would only set their shoulders to the wheel, and do battle in the manner he had sugges- ted, they would, without having to work long hours, be sure to beat all competitors. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN WHITE, in propssing " The Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society, 1 said he thought the Jubilee year would be a good one for the trustees to take into consideration the subject of rebuildingthe school in a better and more healthy situation, Mr. FORSHAW acknowledged the toast, [mil gave "The health of Mr. Percival," the chairman of the committee, who briefly returned thanks. The toast of "The Press," preposed by Mr. R. De.vms, and acknowledged by Mr. ROBINSON, ter- minated the proceedings. • During the evening glees were rendered by Messrs. Rose, Forshaw, Hughes, Short, and some of the Blue Coat Boys, Mr. Anderton gave a trombone solo, Mr. Lowe a pianoforte solo, and Mr. W. Whittaker a selection on the concertina. ANNUAL TEA PARTY.

The annual tea Vt-ti-tit-o-Ok-Pla-c-e-11:t the school on Tuesday evening' when a large number of Blues and other friends sat down to an excellent tea provided by*Mrs. Rose. Mr. N. B. Percival (chairman of the committee) sent a supply of cake and nuts. Amongst' those present were Messrs. W. J. Forshaw (honorary secretary), T. Whittaker (honorary treasurer), P. Morris, C. Ackland, W. Smith, J. Povey, W. P. Chorley, T. Lane, W. Richardson, and J. Richardson. The ladies who presided at the tables were Mrs. Rose, Mrs. Fairclough, Mrs. W. Richardson, Mrs. J. Richardson, Miss E. Craik, Mrs. Shaw.; Mrs. Smith, Mrs. Forshaw, Miss Crellin, Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Chorley, and Mrs. Lane. The rooms had been taste- fully decorated. After tea the tables were cleared, various games were indulged iii, and oranges, cakesi and nuts were distribute& The party, which was thoroughly successful, broke, up at ten o'clock. A hearty vote of thanks'Was by acclamation accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Rose.

The Bishop now went throogh the ceremony of institation in the Commenion. The Vicar, as required, took the oath of allegiance to the Queen and her successors, and the oath of canonical obedience to the Bis- hop of the diocese. He else declared his assent to the 39 articles of religion and the Book of Common Prayer, and made the declaration against simony. The customary prayers were impressively spoken by the Bishop, who con- cluded by placing his hand upon the head of the Vicar, and said a solemn benediction. Singing an appropriate hymn. the choresters, 'followed by the clergy, proceeded down the centre aisle to the entrance of the church, where Arch- deacon Barker performed the ancient ceremony of inducting the Vicar into the possession of the church, with its prie velages and duties. The door was closed and locked on the outside, and the Archdeacon placed the vicar's hand upon the key, at the same time making a declaration of the Vicar's induction into the possession of the edifice. The door was then opened. The conclusion of the ceremony was reached by the Vicar tolling one of the church bells, and the congregation dispersed. THE VICAR OF RUNUORN'S FIRST SEII,MON. The Rev. A. Maitland Wood, the vicar'of Rn-ncorn. "reed himself in "at the Parish Church, on Sunday morning. In the evening the rev gentleman conducted the service and preached from the text" What reward shall I give unto the Lord for all the benefits that lee bath done unto me." Psalms cavil, lltb verse. The vicar sketched briefly the teachings of the Church of England, and alluded to the duties of man to God for the many benefits and blessings he had bestowed upon him. He then passed en to notice the duties which he and the congregation had to undertake. Every layman who had been baptised .was a priest before God, and all of them received God's grace and gifts of the Holy Ghost and opportunities which the providence of God made for them to use these gifts. It was their work to dis- charge their duty, and not merely to receive the grace of God, but to use the grace of God. The priesthood of the laity was a great truth too often forgotten. God forbid that he should forget that every man's vocation in life what- ever it might be, if he did it in a religious spirit it was a re- ligious work. But besides that there was the more directly religious calling to which all of them were called ; and that was to do good in the name of Christ whenever there was the opportunity. He could not do better than try to bring before them the thouaht that he (the vlcar) was not the church. They were the church and he was the officer. People often said they went to Mr. 80-and-So's church. He hoped they would not say that was Mr. Wood's church. That was the parish church and belonged to the people of Runcorn. People also said sometimes "I work for such and such a man. I will do it for him. I will go round and visit a district if be asks me." They should not do that, but should work for God and their own church. Please God they would try to work together in that parish, for how many thousands must there be outside who did not think anything of God Do not let them think that he (the

THE ST. HELEres Tons Ist Yonasuinz.—The St. Helens football team left St. Helens on Monday. morning Week for Yorkshire to fulfil their engagements with Horbury. Ossett, and Manniogham. They arrived at Ossett about twelve o'clock, after a narrow escape in a railway collision close to S. Helene Junction. In their first match, at Osaett, one or two of their team were unable to play through being severely shaken. The ground at Ossett was very hard through frost, and a draw was aeranged, although a splendid and exciting game, was witnessed, the visitors having con- .siderably the bast of the game in all departments, On the Tusiklay thefprdeseded te'llor.bury where they again found the ground in a bad state. Nevertheless the match was played, and Horbnry won a close contest by a try. Har- wood (St. Helens) got over the line, but lost the ball. The St. Helens forwards, as at Oseett. had a decided aevantagc!. On the Wednesday they further journeyed to Bradford to. meet Manningham. but, greatly to the disappointment of both teams and a tremendous crowd of spectators, the match had to be Abandoned, the ground heing.one sheet of ice. The Manningham Committee are likely to arrange another match with St. Helens this season at Bradford.

SANKEY V ROIIGATON (MOSSLEY.) This match was played on New Year's Day on the Sankey ground. The visitors are a club which bold a good reputation in its own district, and tale, coupled with the fact that the previous match betwem the two clubs remained drawn induced a good number of spectoTors to witness the game, which throughout wee of the pleasantest ,description. Houghton had slightly the best of the, game in the forwards, but this was entirely equalised by the superior play Of the home bAcks. The visitors started tna play and they were quickly obliged 'to ave. Some good dribbling by the home forwards Wag next witnessed, and Ashurst obtained a try. Howard next put in a good kick.fort he visitors,but Woolley replied with a splendid run and was only brought down on the line when a try seemed certain. From the following scrimmage however, Eligbley obtained a try, ascl from a very difficult place Bird almost landed a goal. Nothing further was scored in tbe first half, Sankey then being two tries and two minor points to good. In the second half Houghton played up,rnach better and got a try which, however, was not im- proved on,,leavaig Sankey the victors by two tries and thre minors to one try and one minor poiht. After the match the visitors were entertained to a substantial repast at the Coach and Gases, and a most enjoyable evening was spent. Mr. E. Gilbert, of the Warrington Football Club, acted as referee.

div.head: SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the &boots, Great Sankey, on Tuesday afternoon. There 'ere present Messrs. C. J. Ridgway (in the chair), W. Houghton, Cook, S Sutton (clerk.)

div.head: POSITION OF TRH" SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE POSITION OF TRH" SCHOOLS.

The Crank submitted to the Board a debtor and creditor account, showing the amount of money borrowed for the purpose of purchasing land and building schools and mas- ter's residence, ALIO for furnishing the schoole, .ke. They would ho gratified to see that after meeting all claims there still remained a balance in hand of £32 2s 2d, a very satis- factory result, considering the alterations and tadditions they were called upon to make by the Education Department. The architect (Mr. Jos. Nodal) and the builder (Mr. John Eamebottom) have done their Work in a thoroughly con- scientious manner, and the thanks of the Board were es• peciallx dun to the vies-chairman (Mr. W. B. Kerfoot) for the great interest he had taken in the Work, and the time and trouble he had devoted to it. Her Majesty's Inspector of Scheele had expressed himself on the oecasion,of the last examioation as highly pleased with the buildings and general arrangement, and was also of opinion that affairs had been very economically managed. The schools would accommodate 282 boys and girls and 60.infante, a total of 342. .The number at present on tbe .books was about 200, so that there woad' be no lack of accommodation for years to conie. The numbera attending showed a steady increase, and under the efficient management of Mr. Clarke good re- sults might be anticipated. The sum borrowed was £2,686. 5s 6, which was repayable in thirty years, at four per cent. • by equal annual instalments of principal and interest com- bined. The payirierit was due in January of each year, and amounted to £25 Os Pol. That meant, rOughly speaking, 2d in the £ upon each half year's rate, and it wal. anticipated that in a ehort time 3d in the £ would meet all expenses. Owing to re-arrangement by the Education Department in the dates of payment of the Government grant it had been necessary to call for a larger UM for the current year than would otherwise have been the case; still 4d in the upon each half year's rate would cover re-payment of loan and all other expenses without crediting the grant.—this report was adopted.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW SCHOOL AT SANE Y BRIDGES.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW SCHOOL AT SANE Y BRIDGES.

The CLERK also read a letter from the Education Depart- ment, dated 31st December, informing the Board that an application had been made to the Department by Mr. James Suunnersgill for the recognition of a proposed school at Sankey B idges in connection with tie Wesleyan Methodist Church there. The Education Department wished to knew whether the Board concurred in the application. He (the clerk) thought it was evident that the Education Depart- ment were under the impression that Sankey Bridges was under the Impression that Sankey Bridges was within the School Board's jurisdiction ;but he believed that where the school would be erected was really in the township of War- rington. No doubt the greater number of their scholars came from Sankey Bridges, and the new school would inter- fere with them in that respect.—The Cnotattax thought it Would affect them very considerally.—Mr. tiotP3nTotr : Is such a school at all desirable 2—Tie CLERK thought the only reason that could be given for building the new school would be the distance from Sankey Bridges to the Board school. At that school they had plenty of accommoda. tion for some time to come, and one of the reasons why they had secured so much- accommodation was that the children from Sankey Bridges might be provided for. It would consequerttly be hardly fair if they were now robbed of these children. It might turn out that although Sankey Bridges was not under their jurisdiction they still had power to interfere.—Mr. Houghton thought that before they did anything the matter should have careful consideration: and they should first of all inquire as to what need there was for such a school, seeing they had in the neighbonrbood so excellent a seAeol as that Board school.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that the establishment of the new school would affect St. Mary's school more than them.—Mr. HOUGHTON could see no need for the new school, and especially for such a school as woold be built.—Mr. Coog was of the same opinion, and urged that the clerk should be instructed to objct to the new school being erected.—ln the end the clerk was instructed to write to the Education Department asking for the reasons for the application from Mr. Sum- meregill, and pointing out that in that Board school ample accommodation bad been provided for all the children at Sankey Bridges. IThis was all the business of importance.

~ BANK QUAY WORKING-MEN'S MISSION, WARRINGTON. The annual tea meeting and enteetainment in connection with the Working-men's Mission, Bank Quay, were held on Monday evening. About 150\ persotis sat down to an excellent tea in the school-' room, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Long, J. Woolley, G. If assail, Ashley, Oxley, Hough, Williamson, John Hassell, Joseph Monks, and David Monks; Misses Proud and Johnson. The entertain- ment, which was largely attended, Was given, in the Mission Chapel, Mr. R. A. Naylor presiding. In the course of the evenhig a report was submitted as to 'Vile affairs of the mission by Mr. T. Ashley, the sec- retary. At their meeting last year, it stated, they were anticipating great alterations and additions to , heir chapel involving considerable outlay. They then had some little anxiety as to meeting that out- lay, but he was now glad to say those additions and palterations had been made to the entire satisfaction of every one who had seen them, and therefore he I thought they might congratulate themselves. (Hear, hear.) Those alterations and additions, as they knew, could not be done without money, and the entire cost of the undertaking ran up the eipendi- ture to £250 12s 2d, and their income from all sources to meet that outlay amounted to £241 12s 2d, thus leaving them a small debt of £9. However, their good friend and patron, Mr. John Crosfield, with his usual liberality and good feeling towards that institution, had consented to discharge that debt, and for this they felt very thankful to him. (Applause.) Their total income for the past year, including last year's balance of £2 8s 30, was .£3l 15 Hid, and their expenditure £3l 2s 30. Iroth accounts were a little in excess of the previous year's, but less than those of the year 1884, but their balance of this year, 13s Bd, was very much below that of last year, which, as he had said, was £2 8s 30. Having mentioned the various items of expenditure, Mr. Ashley went on to shy that what had been for the committee and workers a very anx- iousyear as regarded the chapel had been brought to a very successful close. They should now start upon another year's labour of love with renewed vigour and energy, and with every hope of obteimng a greater measure of success in the future than in the past. (Applause.) The report was signed by Mr. Joseph Monks, president; Mr. David Hill, treasurer; and Mr. T. Ashley, secretary. The following pro- gramme was then gone through in a very successful manner :—Song, "The anchors weighed," Mr. D. Ikin ; recitation," The bells," Mr. H. Ashley; song, "The old rock," Miss L. Horton; violin solo, Mr. Shakeshaft ; song, "The midshipmite," Mr. G. Bax- ter; song, "Weep not for me," Miss L. Ashley; song, "Goodbye, sweetheart, goodbye," Mr. Ikin ' recitation, Mr. B, rierley ; song, "Golden love," Miss L. Horton: violin solo, Mr. Shakeshaft ; recitation, "The lifeboat," Mr. H. Ashley; "Christmas bells," the choir. , Mr: George Riley ably acted as accom- panist. At the conclusion of the entertainment a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, on the motion, of Mr. Morrics, seconded by Mr. HOUGH.

• The annnal treat to the school 'children was given on Tuesday evening, when about 460 children sat down to a I substantial tea. After werds an entertainment, at which Mr. John Crosfield took the chair, was held in the school-room, which was crowded with children and a number of adult friends of the children. The proceedings having been corn• menced with singing and prayer, the choir gave a chorus. Mr. John letpsall then read the report of the Sunday School for the past year, which, he said, it gave him great plea- sure to present. He would take the earliest opportunity of tendering, on behalf of the superintendents, officers, and teachers, their siecere thanks to all the friends who had in any way helped to cores' on the good Work in connection with that Sabbath School, and at the same time they en- tertaitied the Jeep that similar help would he forthcoming in the future. The offic?rs for the past yeAr were :—Preei- dent and visitor, Mr. Joseph Monks, seuior ; teiperintendente, Mr. R. Williamson and Mr, N. Hough; trea-urer,. Mr: J. Dawber ; secretary, Mr. John ,Hasaall. •Numericilly, the school compared well with precedintryearse The number of scholars Was, males 259, -females 211, making a total of 470, two more than lest year. Toe teachers numbered, male 18, females 8, total 26. The average attendance of, children in the morning was, males 85, females 62, total 147 ; and in the afternoon, males 169, fem dee 148, total 317: This made an average attendance fur each day of 464, The average at- tendanceof Teachers was, in ,the morning 13 males and 2 females, and in the afternoon 17 melee and 5 females. Financially also they were in a very satisfactory position. The treasurer had £4 7e 4d in hand at the, commencement of the year, and the it:come during the year had been £47 3s 10d, making a total of £5l Ile 21. The ex- penditure had been £4B 193 11d, which left a balance in hand of £2 lie 3d. The officers elected for the 'present year were esident, Mr. Joseph. Monks, son.; superintendent.. Mr. John Dawber and Mr. David ; treasurer, Mr. J. Woolley ; secretary, Mr. John Hassell; Mr., Willie neon being viaitor along with, Mr. Monks. They had a Band of Hope in connecioa with the Sunday school, which was very seccessfully Worked by the teacher's and senior scholars. There bad been 31 'meetings in connection , with the Band of Hope, all of which , had been of an in- teresting and instructive character, and well attended. The programme at these meetings was, with Very little excep- tion, carried out bYlithe children 'themselves, and .the parents were induced to come and listen. A Bible Class re- cently started for teachers and senior scholars bad done great ' good. It would be very encouraging to all present to know that the school had .prospered so much duriug the twit year. e (Applause.)— The CHAIRMAN. who was receivel with cheer after cheer, said that be was very glad to meet his friends at that inter- esting tea party. He efid not know exactly 'how many years it was since the school was opened, bat he thought that it must be at beet ten years. (A voice: Fourteen.) He thought from the report just read that the school was ' never so flonrishing as it was at the present' time.. They I Dad bad troubles in that school, as was the case with almost' all schools, but he believed that now peace and contentment , reigned. That school was the first one 'built on that-1 side of the London and.North-Western Railway, and they might . imagine, what was the condition of Bank Quay, Atherton's Quay; and Sankey Green, before it was opened. On a Sunday the children were left to ratriblu about where they choosed. They got no education, and. were left to grow up almost as though they were wild. Surely, during the last fourteen years that •Sunday school must have had considerable inflhance upon the children in that immediate neighbourhood. He did not think that there was any more beautiful sight to 'be found than that of a schoolroom fall of clean, welledrel•sed, healthy looking chil- dren, such ache saw there that night, and that they were clean and well dressed was in itee,lf an evidence of the bene- fits of education. Ak years pissed they would see Imre and more of the good effects that were produced;en that neigh- bourhood by the training that the children got in that Sun- day school. The childrene and tile parents too, owed a deep debt of gratitude to the teachere, who were engaged in a noble and praiseworthy work. He hoped that the school Would Prosper. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfield then distributed to thefollowing tiersons prizes of books for their assiduity in tract distributing :—Messrs T Taylor, H James, H, Kay, 11-Edwards, W Hill, H Warden, John Middleton, and Misses C Ashley, S A. Hassell, C Dunn, F A Hough, It Pitchford, M Tilling, M Roughlev, P Cartwtight, P Jones, and Lee. The progranime subsequently given consisted of pianoforte duets by Master George' Crostleld and Miss Gertrude Cros- field e recitations by Mary Grace, Jane Birch, William Tay- lor, Harry Kay, Lizzie Tilling, John William Pemberton, Emma Smith, John .Middleton; awl Mr Furness; duet by Misses Tilling and Haseall ; song by Clara Williamson ; and songs and choruses by the choir, which was under the conductorship of Mr Frank Williams. Mr T Mills acted as accompanist.

Thursday was the seventy-fifth anniversary of Mn. Gladstone's birthday. Mrs, Gladstone has received several congratulatory messages and birthday gifts. "Mother, this book tells about the 'angry waves of the ocean.' Now, what makes the ocean get angry ?" "Because it has been crossed so often, my son." Nothing is without its special jewel, if only we look for it; and, if we were really wise, we slould find its profitable use in each circumstance and event of our lives. A lady painted a plaque in oil colours and forwarded it to a friend. Soon after a note of acknowledgment came, in which the lady stated that "It is altogether too nice to use every day, so I only use it for a bread plate when we have company.".

King's-road,Fulham,London, on Sundor morning attempted to murder his wife, and then committed suicide, nearly severing his head from his body. The woman:nvho is aged 54, has terrible wounds ontAthe head, inflicted by a hatchet, and is not expected to livg: The Glasgow ~police reported on Saturday that a murder bad been committed in the east end of that city. Mrs Reilly, who •lives at 66, Sarraok- street, was heard to scream and shout "Murder!" The police appeared on tbe scene, and found the woman lying dead in the house, her body being fearfully bruised, while her features were almost unrecognisable. The police, sus- pecting the deceased's husband, who was sitting in the house, apprehended him. At Guildford, on Saturday, George Fuller, a soldier, Alexander Cook and James Dench, la- hovers, were charged with the wilful murder of William Roker, a gamekeeper, on December 26th. A man named Beaver having given corroborative evidence, Deputy Chief Constable Barker said it was believed a fourth man was implicated, and asked for a remand, which was granted. On Wednesday an inquest was held at Fulham, before Dr. Diplook, touching the death of Joseph Williams, a builder's foreman, who made a murderous at- tack upon his wife on Sunday last, and then cut his throat. The jury found that he committed suicide whilst of un- sound mind.

The monthly meeting of this body was held in the Council Chamber at the Town... Hall on Tuesday. The ex. Mayor (Alderman Harrison) occupied the chair, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Davies, Webster, Sutton; Councillors Wright, Barker, Tins- ley, Ashton, Greening, Jolley, Heaton, Bolto_ Nis Green- P'rancombr, Taylor, Marsh, Dakin, Fleming, Roberts; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), Paterson (gas manager), Longdin (borough surveyor). THE LATE MR. J. WARRINGTON WOOD.

The Ex•Mavon said it had been suggested to him a short time ago that it would be an appropriate thing to notice publicly at that Council meeting the death, of the late Mr., Warrington Wood. So far as liewas individually concerned be bad not the slightest objection to it, though, of course, it might be productee of inconvenience if they were to make a point of noticing the death of every worthy inhabi- tant of Warrington. But still this was an exceptional case in which they might be perfectly justified in making a de- parture. As they knew Sr. Warrington Wood was a native • of Warrington, and be (Alderman Harrison.) believed he was right in,saVing that Mr: •Wood was once in the service of that Corporation, as well as his father before him— The career of Mr. Wood had been a somewhat remarkable one. He took his inspiration from Warrington and Warrington's School of Art, and, as they knew, he had raised hinieelf to a high level of artistic distinction, and he had left behind him a great maav works which would record his life's his- tor'. His private life was as exemplary as his artistic life waedistinguished, and there were few who had left a better nama behind them. He required no storied urn to. record the character of his works and his private vittues. His life had been cut short almost in the very midst of his career. A broken column would fitly represent the life of ,Mr. Warrington Wood, for ere he had attained to the maturity of a skilful artistic life he was snatched away by a sudden bereavement, the circumstances of which they were all too well 'acquainted with. He begged to move the following resolution :—"That this Council desires to record its deep regret at the pren,ature death of the late Mr. Warrington Wood, and that by this sad event Warrington has lost one of her most distinguished sons, and art one of her most zeal- ous and conscientious devotees; and also to express its deep sympathy with his widow, Mrs. Warrington Wood, and her late husband's family on the overwhelming atliction that has so suddenly befallen them." Alderman WEBSTER, in seconding the proposal, referred to the gentle nature of the deceased artist, i and to the ab- sence in his character of anything like the inordinate self- esteem wbich some men might have felt under similar cir- cumstances. The resolution was then passed. THE WATERWORKS

The Ex-Maxon said it would be within the recollection , of the Council that there had been a committee appointed to consider the circumstances of the purchase of the Warring- ton Waterworks. They had several meetings, and ulti- mately, with the valuable assistaace of Mr. Alderman Davies, they were enabled to arrive at what they considered to be a conclusion that wou,d enable them to go to the Waterworks Company, to boldly make an offer, subject of course to approval of the Council and the ratepayers, and he had but little hesitation in saying that if it had come before the ratepayers they would in all probability have vetoed—for as they were perfectly honest and sincere in their desire to parched°, they made such an offer as they hoped would be accepted. At all events, it was an offer which he thought nobody would despise,and it was such an offer, that if made by a private person wishing to purchase the waterworks as an investment, he did not think that in- dividual would be considered a very sound financier. But they knew it was not entirely a question of pounds, shil- lings, and peace, but a question that affected the health and comfort of the inhabitants of Warrington. It was besides only right to the Waterworks Company, that they should be allowed to retire from the concern/without sustaininr any loss, and the amount they offered conseqmently WAS considerably in excess of what the whole works had cost, although, as was known, there were some parts of the plant of comparatively DO use. The committee, however, thought it only right the company should be recouped the amount they had spent in endeavouring to supply War- rington with water. The offer was made, and refused, be should think, in five minutes. (Hear, hear.) He afterwards took upon himself to write to Lord Winmarleigh with a view to elicit further information giving his own views of the question and inviting the waterworks directors to make an offer to the Corporation, or rather to say what they would be dis- posed to take for the works. In reply to that letter he had received the following letter from the company's manager, Mr. Ross, viz. :—"December 24th, 18813.—Dear sir,—The directors of the Waterworks Company have had under their consideration the letter addressed by you to Lord Winmar- leigh, the chairman of the company, under date of the 23rd October last, and lam now instructed to reply to it on be- half of the Board. The directors are of opinion that it is not compatible with the interests of the shareholders of the company that any proposition having reference to the ac- quirement of the company's undertaking by the Corporation of Warrington should emanate for their Board. It is,there- fore, impossible for them to adopt your suggestion that they should name terms "on which they would be disposed to sell the works." On the contrary, with every desire to show the utmost courtesy to yourself personally, as well as to the Corporation as a body, the only answer they can make to such a request is that the company's undertaking is not on sale. I am, dear sir, faithfully yours, John Ross, recretary. Joseph Harrison, Esq., Woodbine Terrace, Latchford."—lie (the Ex-Mayor) thought the Corporation had now put themselves in a proper position; and if it should be at some subsequent time necessary for them to seek compulsory powers for the purchase of the waterworks he thought they should stand in a better position than they otherwise should. Having made the company an offer, and that offer having been refused, and then inviting them to tell them what they would be disposed to sell the works for, and that _invitation having also been refused, the Corpora- _ .

tion would be in a position to go with some degree of Moral force to seek for compulsory powers if they should here- after consider it necessary to do so. He did not find any fault with the terms of the letter he had just read, and he had not the least doubt in his own mind that if the property belonged to the present directors there would be no diffi- culty in arriving at a purchase on equitable terms, but of course the directors had to consult the interests of the share- holders.

Councillor TINSLEY : You said something about a pro- pool lion— Alderman HARRISON, interrupting, said he had simply made a communication, but they could not go into a discus- sion of the question that night. Councillor TINSLEY : Then we are to accept anything we are told ? Alderman HARRISON maid it was simply an intimation of whit had been done, but if Councillor, Tinsley desired he could raise the question at the next meeting by giving notice.

THE EXAMINER S.A.DiRDAY. JANUARY 8, 1887.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTE]

1 The minutes contained the following resolutions :—That 1 the drive on the east approach in-front of the Town Hall be k asphalted, and that the borough surveyor be instructed to prepare an estimate of the cost and obtain tenders ; that , the set pavement in Lyme-street be continued up to Messrs. Rowson's premises; thatsthe resignation of Mr. Councillor J. . V. Taylor, as a member of the committee be accepted, and , that the Council be recommended to appoint Mr. Councillor 1 i ' . Fleming to till the vacancy. • Alderman Dams proposed tbefonfirmation of the report of the committee. They had, he said, given insnructions 'for the approach to the Town Hall •to be asphalted, as it seemed to be in accord wjth the request of the Council at the last nrieting. They" were sorry to lose- the services 'on the committee of Mr. Taylor, but had pleasure in appoint- ` ing Mr. Fleming in his, place. Councillor SUTTON seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor !Warm said that ha.,had been recprested.hy several ratepayers in the death-West Ward to draw the attention of the chairman of the committee ' to the bad state of the footpath leading from the old Mill-road to the iron bridge at Arpley. It was in a very dirty and, he might say, unsafe state. . . , ' Alderman WISEST= asked would not wood pavement have been better in front ot the Town Hall ? ' Alderman DAVIES said that the. Toad referred to by Coun- cillor' Heaton was certainly in a very bad state, but it was not within the order and disposition of the Council. It was a private road leading toukrpley,aind was repairable at the discretion of the owners of property in Arpley. He thought that the Council should, notwithstanding, use every en- deavour to get the.road put into better condition, and the borough siarveyor was now in communication with the Lon. don and North-Western Railway Company, who were in some measure owners of propicrty in that, neighbourhood, as it was an approach to their line of railway. As regarded the approach ,ta the TJA Hall they had had a consider- able =Ant df talk, and came unanimously to the conclu- sion to use Asphalt. The minutes were then adopted. ' ECIWOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTIM. . I
This committee submitted the report .of the Inspector,

that 57, cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guar- dians, and school fees allowed in 51 cases for 10lp children. That seven cases had been taken before Vie Magistrates, when a fine was indicted in five cases and two sent to the ship "Clio." [None.-16 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with.] The minutes were agreed to without discussion on the motion of Alderman Webster seconded by Couneillqr Fleming.

The minutes contained the following :—lteport of the Curator for the month of November :—Visitors to the Mos.
earn 2,869 (partlV closed during November 1885,) Books issued in Reading Room 2,212, an increase of .6t! per cent, . _ .
books issued to enbscribere 1,592 a _decrease of 4 .per cent

compared with November 185. The Curator reported var- -ions gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—Minute, that a commu- nication haying been received from the Masi cal Society, offering to present to the Library the collection of music belonging to the society, viz. :—Full snores for orchestra, ' incluchng a series of the publications of the Handel Society, sets of instrumental parts ter orchestra, vocal scores, upon the understanding that the Musical Society have the first claim to the use of the same at any time. It was ressived that the offer be accepted and the thanks of the Committee given to the Society. _ . . .

Alderman Webater, in proposing that the minutes be adopted, called attention to the increase of 60 per cent in the number of books issued in the reading room. The motion having been seconded by Councillor Green. all, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

From the report of the Registrar it appeared that the in- terments for the past fortnight were :—Adul ts, 12; minors, 30; still-born and premature, 6; and for the corresponding period last year—adults, 15; minors, 13; still-born and pre- mature, 7. The receipts for the past fortnight were £36 75 2d; and for the corresponding period last year, £2B 17s 10d. On the motion of the Ex•Mennt, seconded by Councillor TAYLOR, the report was adopted without discussion.

TOWN HALL PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The report of the Beth•keeper stated that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £3 9s, and for the corresponding period\ last year £4 is. The minutes also contained: Resolution, that the best thanks of this Council be given to Mr. T. Garnett, of Penketb, for a present of 00 bulbs. The minutes were confirmed, on the proposition of the EX•MATOR, seconded by Councillor BOLTON. GAS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this coinfhittee stated that the average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 17.45 candles at both works, Alderman Homuns proposed, and Councillor Ashton seconded the confirmation of the minutes: Councillor GREZNALL asked the chairman whether there was any hope that we might have better gas? (Hear, hear.) In Cheshire the gas was anything but satisfactory, and, considering the price paid it should certainly be better. Councillor Mount Said that It' was absurd to say that they, at leasesso far as Latchford was concerned, got gas equal to 17-45 candls power. He thought they should have a better light. Councillor FLEMING said that he could endorse what Mr. Tinsley had said. Last week it was worse than he ever be- fore experienced. There were three lights In his dining. room, and he did not think they got a quarter of a candle ight7 not to speak of 17 candles. (Laughter). . . .

'Alderman 110LMES admitted tat ibere bee been a good deal of complaint upon the question of gas. He did not think that there was any diminution in the quality, for, so far as the records they had shewn, the gas was equal to from 17 to 18 candles but they had had a deficiency of supply. The reason a that was that there had been a large demand upon the gas wores during the past two or three weeks, and they had not been able to put on the pressure they would have liked. It was a certainty that they would not have these compliments much longer. The Ex-fdavon said that he could assure Alderman Holmes that no one would be more delighted than he should be, when there was an improvement in the direction indicated. The report was adopted. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee a letter was read from the Vice-Chancellor of the Victoria University, Manchester, requesting the C, rporation to present a memorial supporting an application for an annuli grant from the public fonds to the Victoria University, and it was resolved that the Conn. cil be recommended to present such a memorial. The minutes were passed on the motion of the Ex. MAYOR, seconded by Alderman Dams. This was all the business.
SEVERE SNOWSTORMS AND FROST.

GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. On Saturday there were taken from the'Birming- ham canal at Tipton the bodies of William Sheldon, aged 9, and James Pardoe, 40, puddler. The boy had been sent on an errand, and the man was on his road home near the canal, when the fog enveloped them. The police had also dragged and searched for a boy who was last seen on the canal , side after skating, A Berlin corresponfloent telegraphs :—ln the king- dom of Saxony, where the recent severe weather has been most severely 'felt, as many as twenty- three persons have been frozen to death during tile snowstorms. Railway communication has been for some days almost suspended, but the lines are now again almost all open, though fresh interruptions are feared. A fatal accident occurred in St. James's Park, London, on Saturday. One of the skaters was seen to suddenly fall backwards, striking his bead with great force. He was picked up insensible and takm to Westminster Hospital, but on examination .t;eing made 11,-; was found t 9 des4. It is suPT;sed that in falling he fractured his skull. Daeased was sub- sequently identified as Thomas J. Rowson, residing at No. 30, Smith-square, Westminster, and his age is about 28.

_ At Heywood, on Sunday, the body of a man named Heap, who had in the fog missed his way, was found in a valley where the unfortunate man had lain until he was frozen to death. One ice aceitlent is of a singularly sad character. Mr. Worboys, schoolmaster, and Miss Hayes, a schoolmistress, both of Cambridge, .who were engaged to be married, strayed into the water at Manea, Isle of Ely, and both were drowned.
There was a complete change in the weather in London, on Monday• morning. After some snow had fallen on Sunday night a rapid thaw set in, and the weather on Monday was wet and miser- able. • .

An inquest was held on Monday, at -Btalybridge, on the bodies on two children named •Tonge, who fell into the canal during Thursday's fog, and were drowned. The mother of the children was censured for sending them to so dangerous a place as the canal wharf during the fog, and. especially after the children had told her they had been in danger. A recommendation was forwarded to the North-west- ern Railway Company, who own the canal, to pro- vide Some kind of fence at the spot where the accident occurred. Sno* fell to a depth of over a foot at Buckingham. Many telegraph wires are (down, and traffic is much impeded. The Post Office authorities notify that telegraphic commu- nication by the Direct Spataislvand all the American Cable Companies is now restored. The vessel to which the East- bourne lifebsat went out, on Tuesday, in a blinding snow- storm, was a Norwegian barque of over 1,000 tons burthen She eventually went on the rocks off Beady Head, and was greatly damaged by contact With the cliffs. The crew were rescued with difficulty•hysthe lifeboat,in sight of a crowd of several thousands of persons on shore, who watched the scene. When the lifeboat returned, after six hours' absence, the men were loudly cheered.
