Xrittro to Mg editor. THE TOWN CLOCK AT WARRINGTON. \ Elir,—Your readers may be interested to learn that the stopping of the Town Clock on Christmas eve was caused by rain having trickled down the rod which leads up to the 'Cal work and rusted one of the bearings. Happening, as it unfortunately did, during a holiday season, the stoppage was not noticed until the Tuesday following. The clock's time-keeping throughout the past year has been eminently satisfactory. On not more than 15 to 20 days out of the 36 have its errors in striking the hour, tested by the Leigh time-signal or Birkenhead gun, exceeded ten seconds.—Yours MONSTTOR.

FREE DINNER MOVEMENT AT WIDNES. 1 Sir,—A short time ago the friends of the little chicks I thought it would be opportune to give them a little picking on Christmas Day. Therefore provision was made in the form of good potato pie and plt3m pudding, and nearly 200 , of the most needy selected by the teachers after careful in- ' quiry into their circumstances were invited to the infant school. Sinam'a Cross, kindly lent for the occasion by the School Board; and by 12-30 there was a very hearty . response on the part of the youngsters, and it was pleasing, to see that they had made themselves as presentable as their ' circumstances would allow. Mr. Showan had been busy at work writing mottoes of welcome and expressions of good wishes appropriate to the season of the year, and these were placed round the room' and gave it a cheerful appearance. At one o'clock, on the appearance of the eteaming pie.!, there was a hearty cheer, and work soon commenced. After the pies the plain pudding was heartily welcomed, and the work of destruction was neon accomplished. Three cheers were given for all those who had taken part in contributing ad providing the same, and the little folks dispersed to their respective home,. The Rev. R. Burdon, who was passing at the time looked in, and made himself very use- ful in serving out to the little ones. On hearing of the movement, I am pleased to say that the following have spontaneously given and sent the following contributions:— Mr. Joseph Longton, Ditchfield Rail, Ditton, 4cvet. of potatoes; Mr. Smart, 17ihs of shin bone; Mr. Riminer, 101bs of beef; Mr. F. Lawrineon, 461bs Pt 'dour; Mrs. B. Sadler. 91bs of fruit; Mrs. Warham, 4t4;lbs of fruit; Mrs' Inns, 'ribs of onions; Mr. Warhain, cloth for puddings; "One who wishes it was more," 2s ; Rev. G. Bond, M.A., se: Rev. R. Bunion. ss; A Young Gentleman, ss; Mrs. Inns. is; J. C., 2s 6d ; R.. 23 ;R. L., la ;J. IL, 2s 6d; Dr. Hurter, la ;G. Davies' 25Si; Mr. William Wood, 103; Mark Johnson, is; for which I tender the thanks of the little ones. I beg also to say that, if it is the desire of the generous- hearted that the movement should be continued en the lines of last season, those who took part in the working of same are willing to act as before. I think I ought to say that a number of girls in the senior classes volunteered to pare and slice SOlbs of potatoes required for the pies. On behalf of the little ones, I am, yours, the , b. B. STRINGER. Victoria-road, Widnes.

_ THE POLITICAL SITUATION- NEGOTIATIONS WITH MR. GOSCHEN. On Saturday morning, the announcement was made that Mr. Goschen had been offered the port- folio of the Chaneellor of the Exchequer. He then had an interview of over half an hour's duration with Lord Hartington, and proceeded to Brook's Club. Mr. Chamberlain also had an interview with his lordship, which lasted for over an hour. During the afternoon it was stated that before giving a Anal reply on a matter likely so seriously to effect his political future Mr. Goschen preferred to take time for consideration. On Monday, Mr. Goschen accepted the position of Chancellor of the Exchequer offered him by Lord Salisbury. We understand that Mr. Goschen has explained his position to Lord Hartington, who fully concurs in his decision. Mr. Goschen spent a short time at Brooks's Club on Thursday morning, but Lord Hartington had recaivLd no visitors up to half-past 12 o'clock. LORD LANSDOWNE AND LORD NORTH BROOK

DECLINE OFFICE. Lord Lansdowne, replying from Ottawa to Lord &lie- I bury's telegram offering him the poet of Secretary of State for War. has declined to enter the Cabinet, not desiring to sever his connection with Canada at present. lhe " Standard " says :—We hslieve that up to the present time no further changes have been definitely made in the Cabinet, though the negotiations are still going for- ward. It is understood, however, that the overtures made to Lord Northbrook have been declined. The " Daily Telegraph" says t--It is understood that no Unionist Peers are likely to join the Government, though it is satisfactory to learn that all who have been consulted by Lord Bartington are perfectly loyal in their determina- tion to support the existing Administration. General rumour points to Mr. Edward Stanhope as Mr. Smith's suc- cessor at the War Office, but the particular post which will be bestowed on Lord Iddesleigh if the Marquis of Salisbury become Foreign Minister has, we believe, not yet been finally determined. Mr. Edward Stanhops has been transferred from the Colonial Office to the War Office. lie successor in the former department has not yet been appointed. The re- tirement of Lord Iddesleigh from the Foreign Office is said to be finally arranged. A Plymouth correspondent says that the noble Earl will never again take office. In the Conservative clubs there is said to be much dissatisfaction with the manner in which Lord Iddeeleigh has been treated.

LATEST DETAILS-. The Prime Minister returns to his ohl position as Secre- tary of State for Foreign affairs, vacated by the resignation of Lord. Iddesleigh. In the case of Lord Cross, who also offered to retire to make way for a Liberal Unionist peer, there is no further occasion for his resignation, and he will probably remain at the India Office. Yesterday, no further Cabinet appointmmte were made. Lord Salisbury came to town in the afternoon, but subse- quently returned to Hatfield. During his stay in London he had an interview with Mr. Goschen and Sir Robert Morier. LORD IDDESLEIGH'S RETIREMENT.

The Central News is enabled to state that there is no foundation for the report that Lord Iddesleigh is leaving the Foreign Off See on account of ill health. The suggestion that he should retire from the Foreign Office came from Lord Salisbury last Tuesday afternoon. It was altogether un- expected, and the suggestion is still under Lord Iddesleigh's consideration that be should tille another pat in the Cabi• cet„ His lordship continues to rixeive daily letters of ad- vice, sympathy, and encouragement from all parts of the Conutrv. It is felt that his retirement from public life Would boa very serious loss to the Conservative party, and strong efforts are therefore being made to induce him ts re- main in the Cabinet. The " Western Morning News" (Plymouth) says it is sot Lord Iddealeigh's present intention to hold office in the assisting or any future Government. It is no secret that he has viewed with some amount of dissatisfaction the pro- ceedings that have taken place in connection with the re- construction of the Government. A. PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF LIBERALS.—PROS- PECTS OF RECONCILIATION.

rirr. GladsLne, haring been asked by a Leeds corm., p )adent whether he has noticed suggestions that a reunion of :he Liberal party was not improbatle, on the condition that some concession on the Horne Bade question was made, =a whether he was prepared to make any compromise up- the vital principle of an Irish domestic legislature,

replies he is aware of no change whatever in his own political attitude, and adds that be was unaware that any uncertainty existed on the stiojecr. The "Pall Mall GAZ.tte" of Monday says :—We are in a position to announce that. as the oulcome of the secret negotiation/4 at which we have hinted more or less vaguely of la's, Mr. Chamberlain has consented to go into an informal conference with Mr. Gladstone, Mr. John Morley, and Sir Win. Harcourt, on the Irish question. The object of this conference will be the discovery, if possible, of a basis of Liberal union on a policy of Home Rule which Mr. Chamberlain can accept, and which will, at the same time, meet the approval of Mr. Parnell. Such a conference Mr. Chamberlain regards as extremely desirable. In view of the approaching Liberal Conference of Con- ciliation, a London correspondent says Mr. Gladstone is not indisposed to make one important concession. The Government of Ireland Bill provided that certain sublecte should be reserved for the Imperial Parliament, but apart from this reservation the whole power of legislation in Ire- land was given to the Irish Legislature. The Gladstonian leaders are not unwilling to revise this arrangement, and to delegat, certain specific queet;ons to the lrish legislative body, reserving all oth.,rs to the Imperial Parliament. This is a rnatedal change, end would possibly go some way to meet Mr. Chamberlain's difficulties. It would ' also make the retention of the Irish members at West- minster an eisier and simpler matter than under the old plan. Anaweriog some questions regarding the letters which some time ago passed between Mr. Parnell and himself, regarding the National Council scheme, Mr. Chamberlain says the scheme was not his, but Mr. Parnell's, and that Mr. Parnell now arinats it.

say, possessors of his pictures are content to lend them for exhibition without charge. But they ex- act very onerous guarantees against loss. Every picture is insured against loss of damage from the moment the agents of the Grosvenor gallery appro- ach them on the walls of their owners to the mo- ment they are reinstated. The total insurance on the pictures in the gallery amount to .E 300,000. Mr. Augustus Harris has invested not less than .Z 20,000 in his latest Christmas speculation at Drury-lane. This, in dramatic circles, is said to be the largest sum ever paid for pantombhe expenses. Drury-lane when full holds .£2OO a night; whence it will appear that before Mr. Harris begins to clear his original outlay the pantomime must run through three glorious weeks. There are, of course, in addi- tion to the capital embarked, the daily expenses, which are enormous. To make a financial success of " Forty Thieves" it must run up to Easter. Can it ? . .

_ At the private view of the Grosvenor, the one face that attracted attention was Lady Colin's. Many people were curious to see whether she would go, and many how she would be received. In one sense the Winter Exhibitions are more fashionable than the summer ones. I mean their private views are more fashionable. It arises thus. The pictures are sent by their titled or wealthy owners, who are naturally most anxious to see how they look amidst different surroundings, and pos- sibly, too, in a better light. Wealth and , aristoc- racy were well represented amongst the guests who were invited to view the Vandycks. Lady Cohn was certainly very much observed. Her commanding height rendered her the more conspicuous. Her dress was quiet; it was the same mulberry-coloured costunie which she wore all through the Divorce Court proceedings. Strange stories are afloat as to what she intends to do. Of course every one has heard, and no one believes the story, that a very large salary has been offered to her if she will sing at a London Music Hall. But that she may adopt the stage as a profession is less unlikely. In the meantime she is keeping herself well before the ' public—a course which some of her friends ap- prove, and others think most injudicious.

RUNCORN HABITATION OF THE PRIMROSE LEAGUE.

The formal inauguration of the Rancour Habitation of the Primrose League of which Lady Brooke occupies the p.sition of Ruling Councillor, took place on Wednesday evening in Runcorn Public Hall. Although the weather was unfavourable the attendance was not se large as might be expected to greet the member of a Conservative Govern. meet. The ball had been tastef ally adorned. Round the gallery were displayed the names of Conservative statesmen. but the name of Lord Randolph Churchill was conspicuous be its absence. The chair was occupied by Lord Eeerton of Tattoo, and he was supported on the platform by the Earl of Dunraven, K.P., Under Sec•etery for the Colonies, Lady Egerton, Lady Brooke, the Mimes Brooke, Messrs. E. Swetenham, Q.C.. M.P., W. H. Verdia, J.P., Jes. Reynolds, J.P., W. A. Gorst, W. L. Evans, H. White, J. Torkington, W. Hankinson, J. C. Crawford (Widnes), James White (Wid- nes), J. E. Meredith, W, Kirkham, J. Benkes, W. J. Shores. Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Liahtburn, Mr. and Mrs. J. Speakman. Mr. and Mrs. Rogerson, Mr. and Mrs. T. Kirkham, Mr. and Mrs. T. Hitchen, Mr. and Mrs. Whittaker, and the Revs. W. Preston, J. Lockwood, John Jervis, and R. Edwards, and Mr. T. H. Annett (who bad cbarge of the arrangements). —Mr. Annett having read numerous letters of apology. the chairman delivered a brief address in which he referred to his former connection with Rencorn as the member for Mid-Cheshire, and expressed his pleasure at renewing his acquaintance with his old constituents. The Primrose League, he said, included alrpatriotic and loyal subjects ir- respective of party and religion—(applause)—and be ven- tured to claim for the League the support of all Conserve-1 tives and all Liberals in these critical timer, when some of the main principles upon which the constitetion was founded were at stake. (Applause.)—Mr. Annett then read the war- rant forming the Habitation, which was presented by the chairman to Lady Brooke, the Ruling Councillor, and the Habitation was declared open.—Mr. W. H. Verdin, who was received with applause, moved the following resolution t —" That this meeting heartily welcomes the Earl of Dun. raven, K.P., to Runcorn, and rejoices at the triumph of the liui n Cause at the last election. It expresses its unabated confidence in the ability of the Government of Lord Salis- bury to meet the present difficulties and to deal jnetiv and firmly with the lawlessness and lawless agitators in Iretill and to hand down unimpaired the glorious inheritance re- ceived from our forefathers." After alluding to the alori- One triumph of the Unionist cause in Northwich Division and to the spread of Conservative principles amongst the working-classes, he said there was no part of the Northwich Division that had made. greater progress ;in Conservatism than in the important seaport of Runcorn. (Applause.)— Mr. W. A. Gorst secoeded the motion, which wets carried without dissent.—The Earl of Dunraven, who had a hearty reception, replied. He said it would be futile to disguise from themselves that the Government and the Conserva- tive party had temporarily received a severe shock in the resignation of the late Chancellor of the Exchequer, but it was important to note that there was not the faintest sign that the slightest difference of opinion had arisen between the late Chancellor of the Exchequer, and his colleagues on any point connected with the Government of Ireland. or in connection with the policy of union. (Applause.) He saw that Mr. Gladstone had taken the subject up in a letter. Mr. Gladstone spoke of the dislocation of the Ministry as likely to cast a doubt on the solidity of that policy, with regard to which the unity and determination of the Government had been so loudly proclaimed; but judging of Lord Randolph Churchill by the past and by the character of the man, he would venture to' stake his head that in all oases in which the union was called in question, they would find the late Chancellor of the Exchequer using the whole of his energy and his great ability to help the Government in its maintenance. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to foreign effairs, Eerl Dunraven said he bad a very earnest hope that under toe able and wise guid- ance of Lord Salisbury the coune:y would successfully steer through the difficulties that threatened to overwhelm us. (Applause.) In commenting upon the colonies, he said the natural tendency was strongly toward union, and the des- patch lately sent by the 'ecretary for the Colonies inviting our great colonies to send representatives to London to,con- suit together with the Secretaries of State for various de- partments on questions such as mutual defence and mutual inter-communication would stand out as a very important landmark in the history of this country. (Applause.) See-eking of the present crisis, he said it was senseless to suppose that we could maintain the united empire if we were not strong enough an-t wise enough to maintain the United Kingdom. (Applause.) Mr. E. Swetenham Also speke in reply to tt, the reeoln- tiOn, and the proceedings concluded with a vote of thank to the chairman, carried on the motion of the Rey. W. Preston.

At the ad- journed inquest on the body of a gamekeeper named Raker, shot by poachers last week at Glendon, Surrey, a verdict was returned of wilful murder aozainst some persona no- known. Three men are in custody on suspicion, and the police have a clue to a fourth who is believed to have fired the shot- ruitpettistG HIS CHRISTMAS DrerEn.—At the Preseot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs A. R. Gladstone and W. L. Evans, John Gore, a farm labourer, living at Knowsley,was charged with stealing a turkey, value 20s. from &and Farm, Croxtetb, the property of William Wright.—After John Caddick, a farm servant in the employ of Mr Wright, had.given evidence identifying, the turkoy produced as one stolen from his master's farm, P.C. Mc- Henry stationed at St. Helens, deposed that about quarter past six o'clock on the morning of the 24th December, he met the prisoner in Knowsley-road, St. Helens. He was car- tying a bag, in which be (witness) found the turkey pro- duced. He asked the prisoner where he got it, and the pri- soner replied "From Richard Appleton, a farmer at Eccles- ton." This statement was ascertained to be a false one, and the prisoner was kept in custody. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge.and he was committed to prison for three months with hard labour.

Peter Caldwell, Peter Chrimes, William Dooley, W. J. Horton, Samuel Jones, Daniel Jones, Noah Legge, James Smethurst, and Councillor J. E. Wright; In addition to these there were also present the Revs. SilVilkinson, E.' C. E. Carleton, J. A. Druthmond, G. Allton, G. D. Wray, and 3'. llewellyn ; Mrs. Harrison, 'Mrs. John Pierpoint, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Thontas Metffis Mrs. Allton; Mrs, Smehurst, Mrs. Massey, Mrs. Rebert Smith (Lovely-lane), Mrs. Thomas Sutton, Mrs. Saul Jones, Mrs. Aylward, Mrs. Whittle, the iMisses Wilkinson, G. Allton, Taylor, le' Morton, Geddes, .Fraser; and Weldon; and Messrs. D. W. Finney, Joseph Taylor, George Riley, R. W. Francomb, D. Rankin, Allton, James H. Smethurst, James Horton, and Shackleton, most of whom rendered valuable assistance. At six o'clock in the afternoon 342 old women had their treat in the shape of a tea, and, with very little exception,, their wants were attended to by the 'same ladies and gentlemen who were so busy at the old men's dinner. Their ages averaged from sixty to eighty years, but few were present whose years exceeded eighty. The oldest old. lady in the room:was Sarah Birch, of Silder-square, Tanner's- lane, who is almost a centenarian, as she claims to be ninety-nine years old. Mary Daniels, eighty- seven years' did, was. the next oldest, and Fanny Williamson, of Howank-street, Sankey Bridges, eighty-three years of age, came next. These three old ladies were afterwards each presented with- a woollen cap, which had been sent to the conimittee by a Warrington ladYliving in Scotland. After tea lan entertainment, at which a number of the public I occupied seats in the gallery, was given. Mr. John ' Pierpoint, presided, and was supported on the plat- form by several clergymen and ladies and gentle- men who take an interest in the movement. A vote of thanks was. passed' to the president, the com- mittee, and the subscribers, and short ad- dresses were given. by the Rev. G. Allton, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, and the chairman. The' Hon. Secretary (Alderman Sutton) gave a financial statement, stating that in 1886 the subscriptions amounted to £74'3s 6d, and at the last year's enter- tainment about .£6- be 9d was received, making, with £59 las 6d balance in hand, a total of £l4O 88 Pd., The expense of providing last year's treat was £76, Os 3d, which left a balance in hand of £63' 19s 6d. It was wished, be explained, in order to make the Institution as permanent as possible, to. always have enough in hand to pay the expenses of the treat.. He mentioned that about 6001bs. of butchers' meat, exclusive of about 24 rabbits, had. been consumed, and' that the subscribers to the fund numbered about 200, their subscriptions rang- ing from a shilling- to a guinea. A few remarks having beeen made by the honorary treasurer, Mr. Thomas Morris, the, programme was proceeded with. The programme. was opened by a selection onthe concertina by Mr. Whittaker, which was an admir- able performance,. which Mr. Whittaker repeated at the beginning of the second part: Mr. Dewhurst next sang "Friend John," and later-on in the.even- in,g "The old oak," both pieces being very success- fully treated, Mrs. Massey contributed twoc songs in an effective manner, these being "The river of years" and "My Uncle John." Mr. Ikin and Miss llorton each gave two songs in their admirable style, those sung by Mr. lkin being "The anchor:a weighed" and" Good bye, sweetheart," and those of Miss Horton "The old lock" and" Darby and Joan." The comic songs, however, seemed to be the most warmly appreciated by the old' people these being contributed by Mr. Mullins and Mr. Heinen, junior. It sheuld, however, be said that the Dutch songs , and a song entitled," The Ship Canal," by Mr,Taylor, A were certainly amengst the most popular, and this ng gentleman as well as Mr..Mullina and Mr. Bellian, a, a was more than once recalled. Mr. W. S. Woods dren presided at the organ, ad • Mr... George Riley at the Atten- pianoforte. inter-

The Bulgarian delegates left London on Friday morning by the 11 o'clock train from Charing Cross for Paris. em route to Bulgaria. AN EVENTFUL NIGIEF IN CkAscresw.--Several fatal acci- dents and serious occurrences are reported to have hap- pened in Glasgow on Saturday night. James Grossart, a tinsmith, fell down some stairs in Stirling-street, and was killed. Richard Miller compositor, also overbalaneed him- self on some stairs in George-street, and was killed. Samuel Henderson cut 'AIS throat with a razor and is dying, and James Ingram stabbed himself in the abdomen and is now lying in the hospital in a precarious condition. A woman named Mary Quinn is stated to have died from excessive whisky drinking, and another woman named Mary Phillips seriously injured herself by jumping from her bedroom win- dow to escape from her violent hu.band. An unknown man jumped into the Clyde and was drowned.

div.head: LATEST NEWs
div.p: LATEST NEWs

The Rey. Herbert Evans, Congregational minister, has been selected as the Liberal candidate for the Caroarvon Boroughs at the next election. " The "Freeman's Journal" publishes an audited balance- sheet of the Irish Parliamentary Fund opened last June, showing total receipts of £7,055. Snow again fell heavily in the West of Scotland on Fri- day. In consequence of this none of the important football matches will be Played at Glasgow to-day. A telegram from Dover states that a fog of considerable density prevailed throughout Thursday night and Friday morning, and has greatly impeded Channel traffic. The announcement is made that Mr. Bradlaugh him- self will take charge next session of the bill giving the option of an affirmation in all cases where an oath is required. It is now regarded as practically settled that Mr. Goechen will stand as the Conservative and Unionist candidate for the Exchange Division, Liverpool. The Liberals have not yet announced any candidate. NEW MAGISTRaTE.—On Thursday morning, at the office of the ceunty sealkeeper at Preston, Mr. William Lee Pilk- ington, of St. Helens, was placed on the commission of the peace for that borough. • THE QUEENSBERRY DIVORCE Strir.—The "Pall Mall Gazette," referring to the Qmeraberry divorce case, save: The case has been taken to Edinburgh for trial,o that , the wife can get a divt)ree on the plea 4if adultery alone. In England, in addition to adultery, cruelty has to be proven before a div:rce is granted. Lady Qmensberry alleges no cruelty. KICKED TO DE&TH:OI3 Friday morning an inquest was held at Stockport Infirmary touchily; the death of an 'elderly man named Howard,/ of Hatherlow, near Hyde. Evidence disclosed that deceased Went into his son's stable at Bredbury drnnk, and was attacked by a horse, which kicked one of his eyes ont and so tramoled upon him that he subsequently died at the Stockport Infirmary. A verdict accordingly was returned. SHOCKING SUICIDE THROUGH BUSINESS LOSSES.--.-A ais- treoming suicide was reported to the Leicestershire coroner on Friday, a retired grocer named John Boulter being band dead at his residence at Belgrave. Deceased bad been un- fortunate in his investments and i•ost heavily. This preyed upon his mind, and patting a string round his neck he 'jumped from a hamper.. The string broke, but remained tight round his throat, calming suffocation. Be was found lying on his back quite dead.

EXTRAORDINARY TOISCrNING CASE AT OLDHAM. An isquest was held at Oldham on Friday afternoon on the body of Edith Annie Berry, aged eleven. The evidence showed that deceased went to the Workhouse on a visit to her mother, a widow., who is a nurse in the infirnmy, on Saturday. The child was taken ill in her mother's bed- room. Mrs Berty, who is in custody, told the doctor that sly 4) thought the illnels was caused by a heavy supper which the child ate the night before. Deceased, however, continued to be seriously ill, and died on Tuebday. He held a post mortam examination, the result of which left no doubt on bis mind that an irritant poison had been adminis- tered. The prisoner w..rit on Wednesday and drew £I3, for amount deceased had been insured. The stomach and Intestines having been forwarded to an expert, the inquiry was adjourned until Thursday next for his evidence. Dur- ing the inquiry the prisoner maintained a quiet demeanour, but when the chief constable asked that she should be I taken to the lock-up she commenced to scream wildly.

• INDIA AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. CALcurre, Franks.--The Queen's Jubilee is to be cele- brated throughout India on February 16th. The Indian Government has written to the various local officers through- out the country regarding the adoption of suittble steps. FOUR MEN HANGED IN SYDNEY. SYDNEY, FRIDLY.—Of the six young men upon whom sentence of i'eath was recently passed for having outr,iged a sei vent girl in the suburbs of Sydney, four were hanged. this morning. The other two have been reprieved. AN IN.DIAN REGENT MURDERED. NEWTON COMMEOATIONAL SCHOOL.—On Monday the annual treat to the scholars of the Sunday school took place In the schoolroom. The attendance was large, and the ladies and gentlemen who undertook the duty of waiting upon the children were kept bmsily employed. After tea, a large number of prises were distributed, to those children who had been sucoessfal in gaining them by regular atten- dance. Several songs, recitations, &a., were given at inter- vals by the children, and the elocution class connected with the place gave a dialogue, entitled "Our elocution class." siumzeTs' BALT. An Niewrox„—The servants in the employ of Colonel George McCorquodale, Newton, and their friends held their annual ball in the Town Hall, on New Year's Eve, owing to the customary generosity of Colonel McCorquodale. Each of the servants availed themselvsa of tha privilege of inviting friends, and about 60 couples attended. Among the lady and gentlemen visi- tors were Colonel and Mrs McCorquodale, Mr and Mrs A. McCorquodale, J.P., Mr and Mrs George McCorquodale, jam, Mr and Mrs Dudgeon, Mrs F. Birley, Jo. The danc- ing commenced about nine o'clock, and was kept up with touch interest until about three o'clock on the following morning. Suitable refreshments were obtainable in one of the ante-rooms, and the dance music was supplied by Stir, rep's band from Warrington.

T HE IMPROVEMENT ACT DISTRICT OF RUNCORN TO WIT. THE CONTAGIOUS DISE ASEA (ANIMALS) ACT, 1878 and 1886. THE DAIRIES, COW-SHEDS, and MILE SHOPS ORDERS of 1385 and 1886. WHEREAS, by the Dairies, Cow sheds, and Milk-shops Order. of 1885 and 1886, it is provided that a Local Authority may from time to time make re4ulations for prescribing and regulating the cleansing of dairies and cow-sheds in the occu- pation of persens following the trade of cow•keepers or dairy- men, and the cleansing of milk-stores, milk-shops, and milk. vessels used for containing milk ;or sale by such persons. Now, the Runcorn Improvement Commis&oners, being the Local Authority for the said district, within the meaning of the said Orders, at a meeting hisld this Second day of December. 1886, do hereby make the following regulations, • which shall come into force on and after the First day of January next : REGULSTIONe. 1 —That any room or place use I for the storage or vale of milk shall not be used or occupied flea living room, nor com- municate by any means with any bedroom. 2 —That all vessels and other uttoslls used for milk, and all other articles connected thsrewith, together with ell tables, benches, and other articles in any room or pace used for the storage of milk. Ac.. shall be thoroughly washed and cleansed every day. ' 3.—That the fl-ors of every place used for the sale of milk shall be washed nud cleansed every other day before ten o'clock In the morning, and the walls and ceilings lime-washed when- ever required. hut at least three times a year, in February, J une, and October. 4.—That all cow-sheds and shippons shall be properly drained, the floors cleansed dal, y, and the walls and roof lime wlaitewashed whenever required, but at least twice a year, in May and October. 5 —That the fl more of all cow ;sheds mu .t be of brick, stone. or other norm-absorbent material. , 6.—That the woeds s, Registered for the Sale of Milk" be painted over the entrance door of every rocm used for the sale of milk. 7.—That all premises used for the purpose of carrying on the above trades shall be open at all times to the inspection I and examination of the officers appointed by the Local Authority. 8 —That all (couplers of such premises shall make proper provision to the satisfaction of the Local Authority for the supply of proper water for all cattle kept for the purpose of the above trades, and for cleansing the floors and utensils used by them. 9.—That every cowkeeper, dairymen; or purveyor of milk shalt give notice to the Local Anthoritv of any case of illness, ' whether or persons or cattle, occurring on any registered premises. 10.—That every cow keeper, dairyman, or purveyor of milk when so required by the Local Authority, or by their duly ep- painted aficers, give a certificate signed by a duly qualified registered medmal practitioner, setting forth the nature of the illness of such person. 11 —There shall be a superficial space for each cow of not less than 31 feet by 7 feet. but, if two caws are kept together, then the spare. may be 6 feet by 7 feet. The passage of the cow-shed Shail, for each cow, he of the width of 3 feet, but if the cows are arranged as in a double cow-shed, then the parti- tion passage may be 4 feet wide. 12. No person shall begin to occupy any building for the purpose of carrying on the trade of a cow-keeper, dairyman, or purveyor of milk, without first giving' one months notice in writing to the-Local Authority of his intention to do so, and without having received the 'Certificates of Registration from the Local Authority. 13.—Y0 person following any of the above trades shall keep any swine in any cow•shed, or other building used by him for keeping cows, or in any millcstore or other place used by him for keeping milk for sale. 14.—T)e manure heap of the cow-shei must be kept In a s•sewered middenstead," and removed at least once during every fortnight 15.—Any person doing anything in contravention of 'the foregoing regulations shall be liable for every such offence to a penalty of live Pdtinds, and in case of a continuing offence to a.further penalty of Forty Shillings for each day after written notice of the offence from the Local Authority. Provided, nevertheless, that the Justices or Court before whom any corn- plaint may be made or any proceedings may be taken in res- pect of any such offence may. if they think fit, adj edge the payinent as a penalty of any sum ims than the full amount of the penalty imposed by the regulations, The Common Seal of the Runcorn ) Improvement Commissioners was hereunto affixed at a meeting of I the said Authority held on thee Second day of December, 1836, by L Philip Bpeakman4Esq., Chairman, r In the presence of 411 E. MARSHALL, PHILIP BPEAEDIAN, Secretary.) Chairman,
